note: Authored copy for Tier 1 cards. Overrides the generated text in packages/ui/src/eventcard.js. Keys are matched against an event title fragment, because event ids are derived from titles and may shift as the timeline doc is edited. NOT historian-reviewed.

cards.what: Excavation on the Vaigai reveals a substantial urban settlement — brick structures, drainage, industrial residues, and graffiti-bearing sherds — on a scale that pushes urbanism in the far south considerably earlier than the standard account allows.
cards.why: If the dates hold, the second urbanisation was not a northern event that spread south.
cards.evidence: AMS dates on charcoal from the excavated levels, with the associated artefact assemblage.
cards.dispute_text: The Tamil Nadu State Department of Archaeology dates the settlement from the 6th century BCE. A 2023 report by the original excavator placed it 8th–3rd century BCE; the Archaeological Survey of India asked for that report to be reworked, and the disagreement between the Centre and the State remains open as of 2025. The question is live politically as well as archaeologically, and this game does not take a side.

cards.what: Iron artefacts from a Tamil Nadu site return AMS dates around 2172 BCE — the oldest confirmed iron in India, roughly a millennium earlier than the Gangetic Iron Age.
cards.why: The south is not a periphery that received iron. It may have had it first.
cards.evidence: AMS radiocarbon on charcoal associated with the iron, from the excavated context.
cards.dispute_text: The Mayiladumparai dates are broadly accepted. The far earlier claim from Sivagalai — around 3345 BCE — is contested: rice from the same intact urn as the iron dates to roughly 1248 and 1155 BCE, and critics point to stratigraphic mixing and to selective emphasis on the earliest charcoal in the sequence.

cards.what: Speakers of an Indo-Aryan language enter the northwest and their language becomes dominant across the north over subsequent centuries. Whether this was migration, a series of small movements, elite transmission, or something else is the most argued question in Indian prehistory.
cards.why: Almost everything about the Vedic period depends on what you think happened here.
cards.evidence: Comparative linguistics; the Rigveda's own geography; ancient DNA from Rakhigarhi and Central Asian sites; the absence of a destruction horizon.
cards.dispute_text: Positions range from substantial migration to none at all, and the debate is entangled with contemporary politics in India. Because the evidence genuinely does not settle it, this event is latent: it does not occur in every campaign, and when it does the game presents it as argued rather than established.

cards.what: Brahmagupta sets out rules for zero as a number in its own right — what happens when you add it, subtract it, multiply by it — and rules for negative quantities, which he describes as debts.
cards.why: Reached Baghdad in 771 and never stopped travelling.
cards.evidence: The text, its Arabic transmission, and its citation by later Indian and Islamic mathematicians.

cards.what: A twenty-three-year-old writes a hundred and twenty-one verses covering arithmetic, time-reckoning, the sphere and planetary motion. He uses a place-value system, gives a sine table, computes pi to four places and calls the value approximate, and states that the apparent motion of the stars is caused by the earth turning.
cards.why: Not one result but a method: state it, compute it, and say when the answer is only close.
cards.evidence: The Aryabhatiya, with Bhaskara I's commentary of 629 that fixes its date and its readings.

cards.what: Akkadian records name ships from Meluhha moored at Sargon's quay, alongside vessels from Magan and Dilmun. A Mesopotamian seal identifies its owner as an interpreter of the Meluhhan tongue, and a Meluhhan village is attested inland.
cards.why: Somebody in Mesopotamia had a full-time job translating an Indus language, which means there was enough traffic to need one.
cards.evidence: Cuneiform records; the Shu-ilishu cylinder seal; Indus-style objects and weights in Mesopotamian contexts.

cards.what: Bones identified by one specialist as domestic horse are recovered from a Harappan context, which would place the horse in India well before the conventional date.
cards.why: The horse is load-bearing for several competing accounts of the second millennium BCE, which is why the bones are argued about.
cards.evidence: The faunal remains, and the disagreement between specialists reading them.
cards.dispute_text: Distinguishing horse from onager and khur from post-cranial bones and teeth is genuinely difficult, and the specialists who have examined this material do not agree. The identification is neither established nor refuted, and this game therefore treats the event as latent.

cards.what: Eleven teeth from nine adults at Mehrgarh have holes bored into the crowns. The drilling is neat, concentric, and confined to the back teeth where it would not show. Some of the holes have wear on their inner walls, which means the people went on chewing with them afterwards, for years.
cards.why: The oldest known dentistry anywhere, done with a flint bit on a bow drill.
cards.evidence: The teeth themselves, from the Mehrgarh cemetery, examined under scanning electron microscopy.

cards.what: The humped cattle of the subcontinent are not descended from Near Eastern herds. They come from local wild aurochs, taken into the herd here, and their genetics separate from the western line long before either was domesticated. Water buffalo follow. The animal at the centre of Indian agriculture is native to it.
cards.why: The economy the whole game runs on begins with an animal nobody imported.
cards.evidence: Mitochondrial and Y-chromosome studies separating Bos indicus from Bos taurus, and the Mehrgarh faunal sequence.

cards.what: Rows of small compartmented rooms are built at Mehrgarh, too narrow to live in and sealed rather than doored. They hold grain. Once a village can keep a surplus through a bad year it can also decide who gets it, and the compartments are not all the same size.
cards.why: Storage means surplus, surplus means somebody decides, and deciding is the beginning of rank.
cards.evidence: The compartmented structures at Mehrgarh, and the differential grave goods in the cemetery beside them.

cards.match: Cotton thread preserved in a copper bead
cards.what: A copper bead from a Mehrgarh burial has corroded around a fibre and mineralised it. The fibre is cotton. It is spun and plied, which means the plant was being processed, not just gathered — the oldest cotton anywhere by two thousand years, and it is in a grave.
cards.why: The subcontinent's greatest export begins as a thread inside a bead.
cards.evidence: The mineralised fibre from Mehrgarh, identified by electron microscopy and published in 2002.

cards.what: Blue stone from a single valley in the Hindu Kush turns up at Mehrgarh, fifteen hundred kilometres away. Nobody walked that in one journey. It moved hand to hand along a chain of settlements, each of which took a cut, and the chain existed before any city did.
cards.why: Long-distance exchange is older than urbanism, older than the state, and older than writing.
cards.evidence: Sourcing of the lapis to the Sar-i-Sang deposits, and the find contexts at Mehrgarh and Shahr-i-Sokhta.

cards.what: Wheel-thrown pots at Mehrgarh start appearing in thousands, standardised, from a small number of production sites. Somebody is making pots full time and eating grain they did not grow. It is the first job in the game that is not farming, and every later specialist — scribe, reciter, soldier — is the same bargain.
cards.why: The first person paid to do one thing. The knowledge economy's whole structure is already visible.
cards.evidence: The mass-produced Mehrgarh III ceramics and the kiln concentrations that produced them.

cards.what: Under a later Harappan layer at Kalibangan lies a field, and the furrows are still there: two sets crossing at right angles, wide spacing one way and close the other. It is the pattern still used in the region for growing two crops in one field, mustard between rows of gram.
cards.why: The oldest ploughed field on earth, and it is being farmed the way a farmer would today.
cards.evidence: The excavated furrow pattern beneath the Kalibangan Harappan levels.

cards.what: Somewhere in the growing settlements a person stops farming and starts remembering. Genealogy, ritual, the account of a boundary dispute, the story of where the people came from. They are fed out of somebody else's harvest, which means the community has decided that memory is worth a share of the food.
cards.why: The knowledge economy opens here, and it never afterwards runs on anything but somebody's surplus.
cards.evidence: Inferred from the surplus and specialisation record; the practice itself leaves nothing behind except its results.

cards.what: Cubical chert weights turn up from the Makran coast to the Ganga-Yamuna doab, and they are all on the same unit — about 0.856 grams — doubling upward and then going decimal. No state is issuing them. Traders across seven hundred thousand square kilometres are simply agreeing.
cards.why: A standard nobody had to enforce. It is the clearest evidence for how the Indus actually held together.
cards.evidence: The weight sets themselves, measured across dozens of sites and found to be internally consistent to within a fraction of a gram.

cards.what: Fired bricks across the whole Indus zone are made to a ratio of one to two to four. That ratio is not obvious and not necessary; it is a choice, and everyone makes the same one, in towns a thousand kilometres apart with no evidence of an authority telling them to.
cards.why: Convention this exact, this widely, with no visible enforcement, is a puzzle no later Indian state repeats.
cards.evidence: Brick dimensions recorded across the excavated sites, consistent to within a few millimetres.

cards.what: Houses are built so that waste water leaves them. Chutes in the wall run into covered street drains, which run into soak pits, with manholes for clearing. It is ordinary, it is everywhere, and it is done for the small house as well as the large one.
cards.why: The most consistently engineered thing the Indus left. It is plumbing, and it is universal.
cards.evidence: The excavated drainage networks at Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Lothal and Dholavira.

cards.what: Five hundred years of cities, and no building anyone can identify as a temple, no palace, no royal burial, no monumental sculpture of a ruler, and almost nothing in the ground that is only for killing. The largest structures are a bath, a granary and a set of walls.
cards.why: Every other early civilisation announces its rulers in stone. This one does not, and nobody knows why.
cards.evidence: The absence itself, across every excavated Indus site — a negative result reported consistently for a century.

cards.what: A sunken brick tank on the citadel at Mohenjo-daro, waterproofed with bitumen, with steps down at both ends, a drain, and small rooms around it. It was maintained for centuries. What happened in it is not recorded anywhere, because nothing from this civilisation can be read.
cards.why: The one Indus building that looks like it was for something other than living or storing.
cards.evidence: The structure itself, its bitumen layer and its drain, at Mohenjo-daro.

cards.what: The weights run 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and then shift to decimal multiples of 16 — 160, 320, 640. Binary at the small end where you are weighing beads, decimal at the large end where you are weighing grain. Somebody worked out that these are different problems.
cards.why: A measurement system designed around what is actually being measured, four and a half thousand years ago.
cards.evidence: The surviving weight sets and their mass distribution, published across the major excavation reports.

cards.what: Sargon of Akkad boasts that ships from Meluhha, Magan and Dilmun tie up at his quay. Meluhha is the Indus. The boast is on a Mesopotamian inscription, which means the Indus enters written history in somebody else's language, before and after its own writing became unreadable.
cards.why: The first time the subcontinent appears in a document anyone can read.
cards.evidence: The Akkadian royal inscriptions, and Indus seals and etched carnelian beads found in Mesopotamian contexts.

cards.what: A cylinder seal from Mesopotamia belongs to a man described as an interpreter of the Meluhhan tongue. Somebody made a living translating between Akkadian and whatever the Indus people spoke. It is the only direct evidence that the language existed as a spoken thing, and it tells us nothing about what it was.
cards.why: A job title is the closest we have ever come to hearing the Indus speak.
cards.evidence: The seal of Shu-ilishu, in the Louvre, with its Akkadian legend.

cards.what: Eight hundred kilometres north of the nearest Indus city, on the Oxus, someone builds a settlement with Indus bricks, Indus pottery, Indus seals and an Indus irrigation canal. It sits beside the lapis mines. It is a colony, and it is the furthest thing from home the civilisation ever built.
cards.why: A trading outpost planted at a source. The Indus network was not passive.
cards.evidence: The excavated site at Shortugai in northern Afghanistan, with its full Harappan material assemblage.

cards.what: Across the northern hemisphere the climate dries, sharply and for centuries. In the subcontinent the monsoon weakens and the Ghaggar-Hakra, which had carried water past dozens of Indus towns, begins to fail. Nobody attacks. The cities become harder to feed, and their people move east toward rivers that still run.
cards.why: A civilisation can end without a conqueror.
cards.evidence: Speleothem records, lake cores, and the abandonment sequence of the Ghaggar sites themselves.

cards.what: The cities empty. There is no destruction layer, no mass grave, no burnt gate, no invader in the ground. Public buildings stop being repaired, the drains silt up, the weights drift out of standard, and the number of settlements actually rises while their average size falls. People disperse eastward.
cards.why: The single hardest thing in this game to render honestly, because it has no villain.
cards.evidence: The excavated upper levels at every major Indus site, and the regional settlement surveys that count more sites, not fewer.

cards.match: Last use of the Indus script
cards.what: Around four hundred signs, on seals and tags and a single large signboard, average inscription five signs long. Then it stops. Nothing on the subcontinent is written again for sixteen hundred years, and the script has never been read — the corpus is too short and there is no bilingual.
cards.why: Literacy is not a ratchet. It can be lost, and here it was, completely.
cards.evidence: The seals and inscribed objects themselves, absent from all later levels, and undeciphered after a century of attempts.

cards.match: Sorghum and pearl millet arrive from Africa
cards.what: Two African crops turn up in Gujarat and the Deccan. They are drought-tolerant, short-season, and they will grow where wheat and barley will not. They arrive as the climate is drying, and they are what makes farming the peninsula possible at all.
cards.why: Somebody carried seed across an ocean, and it reorganised where India could grow food.
cards.evidence: Directly dated sorghum and pearl millet from Rojdi, Babar Kot and Deccan Chalcolithic sites.

cards.what: Two harvests in one year: one sown with the monsoon and reaped in autumn, one sown after it and reaped in spring. It doubles what a field yields and it halves the risk, because two failures are needed to starve instead of one.
cards.why: The agricultural year that still structures rural India begins here.
cards.evidence: The archaeobotanical assemblages showing summer and winter crops together at the same sites.

cards.what: Hymns start being composed in an archaic Sanskrit, by named families, for ritual use. They are not written down. They will not be written down for something like three thousand years, and when they finally are, the manuscripts turn out to agree with each other to a degree no manuscript tradition anywhere else achieves.
cards.why: The longest continuously transmitted text in human history, and it was carried in people's heads.
cards.evidence: The text itself, its internal family books, and the archaic linguistic stratum that separates it from later Sanskrit.

cards.what: To stop the text drifting, the reciters build error-correcting codes into the recitation. The padapatha separates every word; the kramapatha recites them in overlapping pairs; jata and ghana permute them in fixed patterns. A dropped or altered syllable breaks the pattern audibly and gets corrected on the spot.
cards.why: The finest pre-modern information technology anywhere, and it was invented to protect a text from its own carriers.
cards.evidence: The recitation schemes themselves, still practised, and the near-identity of geographically separated manuscript traditions.

cards.what: Full-time memorisers appear, fed by patrons and taught by lineage. Their capital is entirely in their heads, their training takes a decade or more, and when one of them dies without a student, a portion of the corpus dies too. Everything the player does with knowledge for the next two thousand years runs through people like this.
cards.why: A library made of people. It has no fire risk and no shelf life, and it starves.
cards.evidence: The dana-stuti hymns recording patronage, and the shakha lineages that transmitted each recension.

cards.what: One hymn, late in the collection, describes society as a body: priest from the mouth, warrior from the arms, producer from the thighs, servant from the feet. It appears once, in the tenth book, in language markedly later than the rest. Nothing before it says this.
cards.why: Two thousand nine hundred years of argument start with a single late verse.
cards.evidence: Rigveda 10.90, whose language and position mark it as among the latest material in the collection.
cards.dispute: Read by some as a late interpolation describing an emerging order, by others as evidence of a scheme already ancient. What is not disputed is that it is late relative to the rest of the collection.

cards.what: Two assemblies appear in the hymns, and they are not decorative: they meet, they argue, they are addressed by rulers who want something from them. A king who displeases them has a problem. It is the beginning of a two-thousand-year thread that ends at Uttaramerur with names drawn from a pot.
cards.why: Self-government is not something that arrives from outside. It is here in the earliest text.
cards.evidence: The references in the Rigveda and Atharvaveda, and the later Brahmana descriptions of assembly procedure.

cards.what: The fire altars have to be built to an exact area, in shapes — a falcon, a wheel, a trough — that must all hold the same amount of brick. Solving that requires converting a square to a circle of equal area, and back. The ritual manuals work it out, and the arithmetic outlives the ritual.
cards.why: Applied geometry, invented because a god was thought to be particular about measurements.
cards.evidence: The altar construction chapters of the Shatapatha Brahmana and the Shulba Sutras that formalise them.

cards.what: The altar manuals state, in prose, that the square on the diagonal of a rectangle equals the sum of the squares on its two sides. They give a value for the square root of two accurate to five decimal places and explain how to get it. It is stated as a rule of construction, not as a theorem to prove.
cards.why: The relation is here, in a manual for bricklaying, centuries before it is named after anyone.
cards.evidence: The Baudhayana, Apastamba and Katyayana Shulba Sutras.

cards.what: In a public debate at Janaka's court, a woman named Gargi questions Yajnavalkya, presses him twice, and is told that if she asks again her head will fall off. She stops, and then tells the assembly that nobody else there will beat him either. The text preserves all of it, including the threat.
cards.why: A woman arguing philosophy in public, recorded by the tradition she was arguing with.
cards.evidence: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad's account of the debate at Videha.

cards.what: The question shifts. The older texts ask how to perform the rite correctly; these ask what the rite is for, and then whether it is for anything. Yajnavalkya works through it in dialogue, concludes, and leaves his household to go into the forest. The ritual apparatus is not abolished — it is made secondary.
cards.why: The moment the tradition turns and interrogates itself, in its own texts, without a schism.
cards.evidence: The Brihadaranyaka and Chandogya Upanishads, the earliest of the collection.

cards.what: A story tells how Videgha Mathava carried Agni in his mouth eastward, and the fire burned the ground dry behind him until it reached the Sadanira and stopped. It is a myth about clearing forest with fire, and it maps onto the archaeological spread of iron-using settlement across the middle Ganga.
cards.why: A migration remembered as a miracle, and the miracle is a land-clearance technique.
cards.evidence: The Shatapatha Brahmana's narrative, read against the Painted Grey Ware settlement distribution.

cards.what: Sixteen large polities are named, and they are not all the same kind of thing. Some are kingdoms with a hereditary ruler. Others — Vajji, Malla, the Shakyas — are governed by assemblies of heads of families, meeting in a hall, voting with counting sticks. Both forms are competing on the same map.
cards.why: For two centuries it is genuinely open whether the Indian state will be monarchical.
cards.evidence: The Pali and Jain canonical lists, the Anguttara Nikaya's enumeration, and the coin and rampart record of the named centres.

cards.what: Flat pieces of silver, cut to weight and struck with several small punches rather than one die. They are issued by guilds and by cities as much as by kings. Once value can be carried in a purse instead of a cart, settlement stops being a journey and becomes a transaction.
cards.why: Money enters the game, and with it every later problem about who is allowed to issue it.
cards.evidence: The punch-marked hoards from Taxila to the Deccan, and their weight standards.

cards.what: Three thousand nine hundred and fifty-nine rules that generate the whole of Sanskrit from a set of roots and affixes, using metarules, an ordering convention for conflicts, and a symbolic notation for sound classes. It is not a description of the language. It is a machine that produces it.
cards.why: A generative grammar, complete and consistent, twenty-four centuries before the term existed.
cards.evidence: The text itself, transmitted with its ancillary lists, and the commentarial tradition from Katyayana onward.

cards.what: A man from a small assembly-governed people in the Himalayan foothills leaves his household, studies with teachers he finds insufficient, and works out a position that requires neither ritual nor sacrifice nor a creator. He teaches it for four decades in the languages people around him actually spoke.
cards.why: A movement that spread across half the world and left India almost entirely.
cards.evidence: The Pali canon, the Ashokan edicts naming the sites, and the archaeology of the earliest monastic settlements.
cards.dispute: Two chronologies are in use. The long one puts the death around 483 BCE, the short one closer to 400. Both are defended by serious scholars and the game presents the window rather than picking a year.

cards.what: Darius takes Gandhara and the Indus valley as satrapies. Herodotus says the tribute was the largest the empire assessed, paid in gold dust. Aramaic comes with the administration, and clerks in the northwest start writing again — in somebody else's script, for somebody else's revenue office.
cards.why: Literacy returns to the subcontinent after sixteen centuries, and it arrives as paperwork.
cards.evidence: The Behistun and Persepolis inscriptions listing Hindush, and the Aramaic documents from the northwest.
cards.becomes: The Kharoshthi script, derived from Aramaic and used for the next seven centuries; the satrapy as an administrative template; and the road system Alexander later marched along.

cards.what: A script appears, fully formed, writing Indic sounds with an accuracy no borrowed alphabet manages: it is organised by place of articulation, marks vowel length, and handles conjuncts. Where it came from is one of the oldest arguments in Indology and it is not settled.
cards.why: Every script in South and Southeast Asia descends from this one, and nobody knows its parent.
cards.evidence: The Ashokan inscriptions, the earlier Tamil-Brahmi and Sri Lankan drip-ledge material, and the potsherd graffiti that may or may not be ancestral.
cards.dispute: Derivation from Aramaic, from a Semitic source via traders, from the Indus signs, or independent invention are all argued. The phonological organisation is clearly indigenous whatever the letter shapes owe to.

cards.what: A Macedonian army crosses the Indus, beats Porus on the Hydaspes in the rain, and is then refused by its own soldiers at the Beas, who will not go further east. It turns south, fights down the river, and leaves. Within two years the garrisons are being killed and within ten the satrapies are gone.
cards.why: The invasion that changed almost nothing politically and a great deal culturally.
cards.evidence: Arrian, Curtius and Diodorus, working from Ptolemy and Aristobulus, and Nearchus's coastal log.
cards.becomes: The Indo-Greek kingdoms, bilingual coinage with portraits, the Milindapanha, and a Gandharan sculpture that would eventually put a Greek drape on a Buddha.

cards.what: Chandragupta takes Magadha and then keeps going. Within a generation a single administration reaches from Afghanistan to Karnataka: assessed land revenue, state mines and salt, a road system with measured stages, and a bureaucracy described in detail by a text that reads like an operations manual.
cards.why: The first time the subcontinent is governed as one thing, and the template every later empire cites.
cards.evidence: The Arthashastra tradition, Megasthenes via later authors, the Ashokan edict distribution, and the Mauryan coin and pottery record.

cards.what: Land is measured, classified by soil and water, and assigned a rate. Villages are counted and grouped. The Arthashastra specifies what the record should contain down to the number of taxpayers, the livestock and the people exempt. A state that knows this can borrow against next year's harvest.
cards.why: Measurement is the state's first and most consequential technology.
cards.evidence: The Arthashastra's revenue chapters, and the Mahasthan and Sohgaura relief orders that presuppose a record.

cards.what: A Seleucid ambassador lives at the Mauryan capital and writes it up: a city nine miles long behind a timber palisade with five hundred and seventy towers, an administration of committees, a claim that Indians do not enslave one another. His book is lost; we have it only in the quotations of people who found it interesting.
cards.why: The first sustained outside description of India, and it survives only in fragments of other people's books.
cards.evidence: Quotations of the Indica in Strabo, Arrian, Diodorus and Pliny, and the excavated palisade timbers at Bulandi Bagh.

cards.what: Ashoka takes Kalinga at a cost he later gives as a hundred thousand killed, many times that dead of the consequences, and a hundred and fifty thousand deported. He then has an account of his own remorse carved on rock, in public, across his empire, and instructs his descendants not to do it again.
cards.why: No other ancient ruler published their regret. It is the most unusual document in the ancient world.
cards.evidence: The thirteenth rock edict, in the conqueror's own words, at multiple sites.
cards.becomes: The dhamma policy, the officers of moral administration, the missions to Sri Lanka and the Hellenistic kings, and an empire that stopped conquering.

cards.what: A ruler has his instructions cut into rock faces across the subcontinent, in the local language, in Brahmi and Kharoshthi and at Kandahar in Greek and Aramaic. They are addressed to the population, not to officials. Writing returns to India as public speech, sixteen centuries after it disappeared.
cards.why: The first Indian texts we can read, and they are a king talking to everybody.
cards.evidence: The edicts themselves, at more than thirty sites, several still in situ.

cards.what: A mission crosses to the island and the canon goes with it, carried in memory. It takes root, it acquires an institution to maintain it, and two centuries later, when famine and war threaten the reciters, that institution writes it down. The mainland's own version of the same texts will not survive.
cards.why: The single most consequential export in the game, and it was a person carrying words.
cards.evidence: The Sri Lankan chronicles, the Ashokan missionary record, and the Mahavihara's own transmission accounts.

cards.what: Famine and war have thinned the reciters who carry the Pali canon, and the community judges that the chain may break. So they write it down — the whole canon, on palm leaf, at a cave monastery in the Sri Lankan hills. It is a deliberate act of redundancy against a risk they could see coming.
cards.why: The clearest historical instance of the mechanic this whole game is built on, and it worked.
cards.evidence: The Sri Lankan chronicle accounts, and the survival of the Pali canon itself when its mainland recensions did not.

cards.what: Sailors work out that the southwest monsoon will carry a ship straight across the Arabian Sea and the northeast will bring it back. The crossing stops being a coastal crawl of months and becomes a run of weeks. The volume of Roman trade with India multiplies within a generation.
cards.why: A wind pattern, correctly understood, does more for trade than any treaty.
cards.evidence: The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, and the sharp rise in Roman material at Indian coastal sites.

cards.what: An anonymous Greek-speaking merchant writes a practical handbook to the Indian Ocean: which ports, which season, what they want, what they have, who to deal with, where the pirates are. It names Barygaza, Muziris, Nelkynda and the Ganges, and it is written to be used, not admired.
cards.why: The best single source on ancient Indian Ocean trade is a working sailor's notes.
cards.evidence: The Periplus text itself, corroborated by the Muziris papyrus and the excavated port assemblages.

cards.what: Sculptors in the northwest begin representing the Buddha as a person. For three centuries he had been shown by absence — an empty seat, a footprint, a parasol. Now there is a face, with Hellenistic drapery, a Central Asian patron paying for it, and an Indian subject.
cards.why: A visual language assembled out of three traditions, funded by invaders, for a religion that had refused images.
cards.evidence: The Gandharan corpus, its Kushan-period dedicatory inscriptions, and the parallel and independent Mathura school.

cards.match: Buddhism moves along the Silk Road
cards.what: Monks and merchants travel the same roads. Texts go north into Central Asia and then east into China, where they are translated by teams working from memory and manuscript together. Within centuries the Chinese canon holds works whose Sanskrit originals will not survive at home.
cards.why: The corpus starts existing outside the country that made it. That redundancy is what saves it.
cards.evidence: The Chinese translation catalogues with their dated entries, and the Central Asian manuscript finds.

cards.what: Two and a half thousand poems survive in eight anthologies and ten long songs, by four hundred and seventy-three named poets, of whom a substantial number are women. They are secular, specific and unsentimental: love in five named landscapes, war, patronage, and the poet's own opinion of the patron.
cards.why: The oldest literature in an Indian language other than Sanskrit, and it is nothing like it.
cards.evidence: The anthologies themselves with their colophons naming poets, patrons and the landscape of each poem.

cards.what: Thirteen hundred and thirty couplets, seven words each, on virtue, wealth and love. It names no god, no caste, no king and no place. It has been claimed since by Hindus, Jains, Buddhists and Christians, and it is the only text in India that all of them can quote without conceding anything.
cards.why: A moral text that survives by refusing to say which side it is on.
cards.evidence: The text and its earliest commentaries, and the Sangam-adjacent language that dates it.

cards.what: A monastery is endowed near Rajgir and then endowed again, by successive rulers, until it is a walled complex of eleven monasteries and six temples with a library of several storeys. Students come from China, Korea, Tibet, Central Asia and Southeast Asia. Entry is by examination at the gate.
cards.why: For seven hundred years the largest concentration of texts and teachers in the eastern world.
cards.evidence: The excavated ground plan, the seals naming the mahavihara, and the accounts of Xuanzang and Yijing who both studied there.

cards.what: Brahmagupta sets out rules for calculating with zero and with negative quantities: what happens when you add them, subtract them, multiply them. Debts and fortunes, in his terms. He gets division by zero wrong, and says what he thinks it is, which means the question had been asked.
cards.why: Zero stops being a placeholder and becomes a number you can do arithmetic with.
cards.evidence: The Brahmasphutasiddhanta of 628, and its transmission to Baghdad within a century and a half.

cards.what: A Chinese monk crosses the Taklamakan without permission, spends more than a decade in India, studies at Nalanda under its abbot, argues in public debate, and goes home over the mountains with six hundred and fifty-seven manuscripts and a travelogue that later archaeologists use as a field guide.
cards.why: A third of what survives of Indian Buddhist thought survives because one man carried it out.
cards.evidence: His Records of the Western Regions, his biography by Huili, and the Chinese translations he then supervised.

cards.what: Rulers begin giving away not land but the revenue of land, in perpetuity, engraved on copper so it cannot be denied later. Temples and brahmin settlements become landlords. Within centuries a large share of the surplus is being collected by institutions rather than by the state that alienated it.
cards.why: The fiscal decision that produces the temple economy, the agrahara, and the endowment the player will spend the rest of the game managing.
cards.evidence: The copper-plate grant series, which run in the tens of thousands from the fourth century onward.

cards.what: A stone at Halmidi records a grant of land to a warrior, and it does so in Kannada. The language had been spoken for centuries and written on nobody's authority; this is where it enters the record and does not leave it again.
cards.why: A regional language becomes a written one, and the map of who can be addressed changes.
cards.evidence: The Halmidi pillar itself, and the letter forms that date it against the Kadamba inscription series.

cards.match: Indian numerals and Brahmagupta reach Baghdad
cards.what: An Indian embassy brings astronomical texts to the Abbasid court. Al-Fazari translates them. The place-value system with a symbol for zero goes into Arabic mathematics, and from there, four centuries later, into Europe, where it will be called Arabic.
cards.why: The most widely used piece of Indian intellectual property in the world, and it travelled as a diplomatic gift.
cards.evidence: The Arabic accounts of the embassy, Al-Fazari's Zij al-Sindhind, and the subsequent Arabic mathematical tradition.

cards.what: A teacher argues that the distinction between the self and the ground of being is not real, writes commentaries on the Upanishads, the Gita and the Brahma Sutras, debates his way across the subcontinent, and founds four monasteries at the compass points — institutions built to outlast him.
cards.why: The institutional innovation matters as much as the philosophy: he built something designed to keep running.
cards.evidence: The bhasyas themselves, and the four matha traditions with their succession lists.
cards.dispute: The dates are argued within a range of a century or more, and the traditional biographies are late and hagiographic. The matha foundation accounts are contested even within the tradition.

cards.what: Merchant associations acquire written charters, their own guards, their own courts, and inscriptions recording their donations from Karnataka to Sumatra. They lend, they insure, they negotiate with rulers, and they outlive several of the dynasties they dealt with.
cards.why: The trust ladder's top rung: a merchant body with legal standing that a king has to bargain with.
cards.evidence: The guild inscriptions across the peninsula and in Southeast Asia, including the Barus inscription in Sumatra.

cards.what: A village near Kanchipuram cuts its own constitution into its temple wall: who may stand for the committees that run the tanks, the gardens, the gold and the courts, and how they are chosen — names on palm leaf, drawn from a pot by a child. Anyone with unaudited accounts is disqualified, and terms are capped.
cards.why: Election by lot, with eligibility rules and term limits, cut in stone because it was ordinary.
cards.evidence: The inscriptions themselves, still on the temple wall at Uttaramerur.

cards.what: A temple is finished at Thanjavur with a tower sixty metres high, built without mortar, and its walls are then covered in inscriptions: land granted, revenue assigned, and the staff listed by name — four hundred dancers, singers, drummers, accountants, garland-makers, each with a house and a share of paddy.
cards.why: The best-documented institution in pre-modern India, and the record is on the outside of the building.
cards.evidence: The temple's own inscriptions, which name its employees individually and state what each was paid.

cards.what: Kulottunga abolishes tolls, and is called Sungam Tavirtta — he who abolished tolls — for the rest of his reign and afterwards. The gain is not in the toll revenue forgone but in the traffic that stops paying to pass, and the inscriptions treat it as the achievement of the reign.
cards.why: A ruler remembered by a tax he did not collect.
cards.evidence: The epithet in his own inscriptions, and the Chola revenue record before and after.

cards.what: A Chola fleet crosses the Bay of Bengal, raids the ports of the Srivijayan empire down the Malacca strait, and comes home. It is not a conquest and it is not followed by occupation. It is about who controls the passage of goods between China and the west.
cards.why: The only transoceanic invasion ever launched from India, and it was a trade dispute.
cards.evidence: The Tanjore inscription listing the ports taken, and the Chinese record of Srivijayan and Chola embassies before and after.
cards.becomes: A Bay of Bengal reorganised around Chola-protected routes, the Ayyavole guild operating from Java to the Gulf, and an embassy of seventy-two merchants at the Song court in 1077.

cards.match: Basava and the Sharanas; the Anubhava Mantapa
cards.what: A minister founds a hall where anyone may speak, and washerwomen, cobblers, boatmen and ferrymen compose short signed prose-poems in spoken Kannada about work, god and the futility of temples. When the movement sanctions a marriage across caste, the state answers with violence and it scatters.
cards.why: The most radical thing in the medieval record, written by the people it was about, and signed.
cards.evidence: The vachana corpus with its authors' signature phrases, and the accounts of the movement's dispersal.

cards.what: Kalhana writes a history of Kashmir that names its sources, weighs them, dates by reign, criticises kings including recent ones, and states outright that a historian should be free of love and hatred. It is not a chronicle of a dynasty. It is an argument about what happened.
cards.why: The first work in Sanskrit that is recognisably history in the modern sense.
cards.evidence: The text itself, with its stated method, and Stein's later verification of its topography on the ground.

cards.what: A raiding force under Bakhtiyar Khalji takes the monastic city. Vikramashila and Odantapuri follow. These were not only monasteries but the largest libraries in the eastern world, holding texts that existed nowhere else because nobody had needed them to.
cards.why: What is not copied out beforehand is not recoverable afterwards.
cards.evidence: Persian chronicles written for the victors; a destruction layer at the site; and the negative evidence of texts that survive only in Tibetan and Chinese translation.
cards.becomes: Tibetan monasteries inherit the curriculum, and the Pala scholarly tradition continues abroad for centuries.

cards.what: Muhammad of Ghor returns a year after losing, attacks at dawn while the opposing army is still forming, and wins. Within fourteen years there is a sultanate at Delhi. The change is not that a battle was lost but that this time the victor stayed.
cards.why: The hinge of the medieval period, and it turns on somebody deciding not to go home.
cards.evidence: The Persian chronicles, and the abrupt change in the epigraphic and numismatic record across the north.
cards.becomes: The Delhi Sultanate; Persian as a court and literary language; Amir Khusrau writing in it and in Hindavi; the Indo-Islamic building tradition; and paper, which cut the cost of a copy by an order of magnitude.

cards.what: Paper mills appear and the price of a written page falls. Palm leaf lasts three hundred years in good conditions and has to be recopied; paper is cheaper to make, faster to write on, and can be bound. The number of surviving manuscripts from after this date is not slightly larger. It is an order of magnitude larger.
cards.why: The biggest change to the knowledge economy between writing and printing, and nobody fought over it.
cards.evidence: The shift in surviving manuscript supports, the mills recorded at Daulatabad and in Kashmir, and the manuscript survival curve.

cards.what: Muhammad bin Tughlaq issues brass and copper tokens to circulate at the value of silver. The idea is sound and would be ordinary six centuries later. The execution is not: the tokens are easy to copy, the state cannot police the forgeries, and within four years the treasury is buying them back at face value.
cards.why: A fiat currency in 1330, defeated not by the economics but by the anti-counterfeiting.
cards.evidence: The tokens themselves, and Barani's account of forgery on a scale the state could not match.

cards.what: A city is laid out among granite hills on the Tungabhadra, and grows into one of the largest in the world — a royal centre, a sacred centre, aqueducts, a bazaar street more than a kilometre long, and a water supply engineered for a quarter of a million people in a basin with no perennial rain.
cards.why: The last great pre-colonial imperial capital in the south, and it lasted two hundred and thirty years.
cards.evidence: The surviving urban core, the Portuguese and Persian eyewitness accounts, and the Sangama and Tuluva inscription series.
cards.dispute: The founders' origin, and the account of their conversion at Delhi and return, is a long-running argument that the sources do not settle.

cards.what: Dara Shikoh has fifty Upanishads translated into Persian, arguing that they are the hidden book the Quran refers to. A Latin version made from that Persian reaches Europe in 1801, where Schopenhauer reads it and says it has been the consolation of his life.
cards.why: The Upanishads reach Europe by way of a Mughal prince and a Latin translator, not by way of Sanskrit.
cards.evidence: The Sirr-i-Akbar manuscript, and Anquetil-Duperron's Latin Oupnek'hat of 1801.

cards.what: An administrative account of an empire: revenue by district and by crop, prices, wages, the strength of the army, the salaries of officials, the procedures of every department, the leading painters listed by name. It is the most detailed statistical description of any pre-modern state anywhere. It is also written to impress.
cards.why: A state describing itself in numbers, four hundred years before that was normal.
cards.evidence: The text itself, and the revenue records that corroborate parts of it.

cards.what: A short engagement decided mostly by an agreement made beforehand, followed eight years later by a grant of the diwani — the right to collect the revenue of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. A trading company stops shipping silver to buy Indian goods and starts buying them with Indian taxes.
cards.why: The moment the trade balance reverses, and it is an accounting fact before it is a policy.
cards.evidence: The Company's correspondence, the treaty with Mir Jafar, and the 1765 grant of the diwani.
cards.becomes: A company with an army and a revenue base, and, within a century, the government of the subcontinent.

cards.what: The rains fail twice. Something like a third of the population of Bengal dies. The Company's revenue records for the same years show collection maintained, and in places increased, because the assessment had been fixed against the land and not against the harvest.
cards.why: The records are the Company's own, and they show what was being collected while people starved.
cards.evidence: The Company's revenue accounts, the contemporary correspondence, and the district mortality estimates.

cards.what: A chain of triangles is measured from Cape Comorin to the Himalaya, correcting for the curvature of the earth and the gravitational pull of the mountains themselves. Radhanath Sikdar, computing in Calcutta, works out that one particular peak is the highest on earth.
cards.why: The most accurate survey on earth at the time, and also the instrument of taxation and troop movement.
cards.evidence: The Survey's own records and triangulation data, and the observatory and computing office registers.

cards.what: A member of the Governor-General's council writes that a single shelf of a good European library is worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia, and concedes in the same paragraph that he has read none of it. Education funding is redirected to English within months.
cards.why: A policy that shaped a century, argued from an admitted absence of knowledge.
cards.evidence: The Minute itself, and the English Education Act that followed it in 1835.

cards.what: Ambedkar is invited to address a reform conference, sends his text in advance, and the invitation is withdrawn because of what it says. He prints it himself. It argues that caste cannot be reformed out of existence while the texts that authorise it retain authority.
cards.why: Written to be spoken, refused a platform, printed at the author's expense, and it outlasted the platform.
cards.evidence: The printed text, and the correspondence with the Jat-Pat Todak Mandal that cancelled the address.

cards.what: Power transfers at midnight. A boundary drawn in five weeks by a lawyer who had never been to India separates provinces, districts, villages and in some places fields. Somewhere between ten and twenty million people move, and several hundred thousand to a million and a half do not arrive.
cards.why: The campaign ends here. Not on a victory screen.
cards.evidence: The Indian Independence Act, the Radcliffe award and its maps, and the refugee and mortality records.

cards.what: Meltwater from a collapsing North American ice sheet floods the Atlantic and the planet cools for a century and a half. In the subcontinent the monsoon weakens. The first farming villages have just been founded, and their first test is a global one they cannot see, name or predict.
cards.why: The ancient game's antagonist introduces itself early, and it has no face.
cards.evidence: Greenland ice cores, Arabian Sea sediments, and speleothem records from Oman and northeast India.

cards.what: At the foot of the Bolan Pass a village grows wheat and barley, herds goats and sheep, and builds in mudbrick — before pottery, which is why the period is called aceramic. They store grain in compartmented rooms and bury their dead with tools and young goats.
cards.why: Everything in this game descends from a village of a few hundred people doing this.
cards.evidence: The Mehrgarh excavation, period I, with its houses, granaries and cemetery.

cards.what: Long before the cities, the Sutlej swings west and joins the Indus, leaving the Ghaggar to run on rain and the Siwalik streams alone. The river the Harappans will later settle along is already living on a reduced income. When the monsoon weakens millennia later, there is no glacier behind it to make up the difference.
cards.why: The river's fate is set four thousand years before the cities that will depend on it.
cards.evidence: Palaeochannel mapping and dating of the Sutlej's avulsion, published from satellite and sediment studies.
cards.dispute: How much water the Ghaggar carried in Harappan times, and whether it deserves the name Sarasvati, is one of the most politically loaded arguments in Indian archaeology. The game presents the hydrology and does not adjudicate the identification.

cards.what: Containers change everything downstream of them: storage, cooking, carrying, trade. The first pots at Mehrgarh are pressed over baskets and carry the basket's weave; within centuries they are wheel-finished and made in quantity.
cards.why: The first synthetic material in the subcontinent's record, and the archaeologist's clock ever after.
cards.evidence: The Mehrgarh II ceramic sequence, from basket-marked to wheel-finished.

cards.match: Lahuradewa: rice at the eastern edge
cards.what: Pottery with rice husk in its fabric, and charred grains, at a lake-edge site in the middle Ganga plain — very early, and far from any western influence. It is argued as an independent domestication: rice entering cultivation here, on its own, from local wild stands.
cards.why: If rice was domesticated here independently, the subcontinent has two separate agricultural origins.
cards.evidence: The Lahuradewa dates and archaeobotany, set against the genetics of indica and japonica rice.
cards.dispute: Whether the early Lahuradewa rice is domesticated or gathered wild is contested, and the genetics complicate every simple story: indica rice later hybridised with japonica arriving from China. Dates and domestication status are both argued.

cards.what: Beads hammered from native copper are one thing; ore roasted and reduced to metal is another. Smelting means furnaces, charcoal, and control of temperature and air — pyrotechnology beyond anything pottery needs. Once you can smelt copper, bronze, and eventually iron, are questions of time.
cards.why: The metallurgical ladder's first rung, and every later rung stands on it.
cards.evidence: Slag and furnace evidence from the Chalcolithic sites, and the compositional analyses of early copper objects.

cards.what: On the Deccan plateau, cattle herders pen their animals inside enclosures and periodically burn the accumulated dung in fires hot enough to vitrify it. They do this seasonally, at the same places, for centuries, until the mounds of burnt ash stand metres high and are visible from far off.
cards.why: Monuments made of burnt cow dung, by people who measured wealth in cattle. Nobody fully knows why.
cards.evidence: The excavated ashmounds at Utnur, Kupgal and Kodekal, with their vitrified layers and radiocarbon dates.

cards.what: A hunting camp in Rajasthan starts keeping domestic sheep and goats — and does not settle down, does not farm, does not build. They take the one piece of the Neolithic package that fits a mobile life and decline the rest, for a thousand years.
cards.why: The Neolithic is not a package deal. People chose from it, and some chose almost none of it.
cards.evidence: The Bagor faunal sequence: domestic caprines inside a microlithic hunter-gatherer toolkit.

cards.match: The sea stands two metres higher
cards.what: In the mid-Holocene the sea stands higher than today, and the Rann of Kutch is a navigable gulf. Places that are now salt desert are coastline; Dholavira's island is an island in water, not in salt. The map the first coastal societies knew is not the map the player is shown today.
cards.why: The coastline is a variable, not a constant, and the game's geography has to move.
cards.evidence: Relative sea-level curves for the western coast, and the marine sediments under the Rann.

cards.what: Little clay carts with solid wheels appear in the villages — toys, or models, of a real thing. A cart means a draught animal, a yoke, an axle, and a path wide enough to use it on. Overland bulk transport enters the economy, four thousand years before roads are anyone's policy.
cards.why: The bullock cart arrives, and it will still be moving India's grain in 1947.
cards.evidence: The terracotta models from Harappa's early levels and the Chalcolithic sites.

cards.match: Rehman Dheri laid out on a grid
cards.what: Centuries before the mature cities, a town in the Gomal plain is built to a plan: a rectangle, walled, with streets crossing at right angles. Whoever built it had decided what a town should look like before laying the first brick.
cards.why: Urban planning precedes urbanism. The idea of the grid is older than the cities famous for it.
cards.evidence: The site plan of Rehman Dheri, visible in excavation and from the air.

cards.what: Signs scratched on pots before firing multiply across the Early Harappan settlements — single marks at first, then combinations. They are not yet writing. They are ownership, contents, tally, workshop. Writing systems tend to grow out of exactly this.
cards.why: The script's ancestry, in graffiti on the shoulders of storage jars.
cards.evidence: The pre-firing graffiti corpus from Harappa, Kalibangan and Kot Diji, and its overlap with later Indus signs.

cards.what: Cotton stops being a wild plant people pick and becomes a crop people sow. It wants heat, a long season and much water, and it repays the investment in something no food crop offers: cloth. From here to the Lancashire looms is one unbroken thread.
cards.why: The subcontinent's defining cash crop enters cultivation. It never afterwards leaves the story.
cards.evidence: Archaeobotanical cotton from Mehrgarh and the early Harappan sites, and the later Indus textile impressions.

cards.what: Signs begin appearing incised on pottery that will later standardise into the seal script — the same forms, the same combinations. Whatever the system is, it is being worked out here, in the centuries before the cities, not invented in them.
cards.why: Writing systems are built, not born. This is the construction site.
cards.evidence: The Early Harappan sign-bearing sherds and their continuity with the mature seal corpus.

cards.what: Craftsmen learn to paint patterns on carnelian with alkali and heat them until the design burns white into the stone. The technique is distinctive, the product unmistakable, and etched carnelian beads from the Indus turn up in royal graves in Mesopotamia.
cards.why: A signature export: a product only one civilisation could make, found in another's tombs.
cards.evidence: The etched bead corpus, the workshop debris at Chanhudaro, and the finds in the Ur royal cemetery.

cards.what: Within a century or two, towns across seven hundred thousand square kilometres are rebuilt to a shared idea: a raised citadel and a lower town, cardinal streets, standard bricks, drains. The convergence is fast and it is everywhere, and no palace or king's grave explains who decided.
cards.why: The threshold the whole era is named for: planning replaces accretion, at continental scale.
cards.evidence: The near-simultaneous mature-phase rebuilding at Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira, Kalibangan and Rakhigarhi.

cards.what: About four hundred signs, written mostly right to left, on seals, tags, tablets and one public signboard. The average inscription is five signs long. There is no bilingual, no long text, and no agreement on the language behind it — or whether there is a language behind it at all.
cards.why: The most famous unread script on earth, and the game must show it without pretending to read it.
cards.evidence: The full inscription corpus of roughly four thousand objects, and a century of failed decipherments.
cards.dispute: Every decipherment so far has failed to convince. A minority position holds the signs are not writing at all but emblems; most researchers think they encode language. The game shows the signs and takes no side.

cards.what: A bronze figure ten centimetres tall: a girl, naked but for bangles, hand on hip, head tilted, entirely at ease. She is cast by the lost-wax process, which means modelling in wax, investing in clay, burning out, and pouring — a mature technology, used here for something with no obvious function except itself.
cards.why: The most self-possessed object in Indian archaeology, and it is a teenager standing however she likes.
cards.evidence: The figure itself, from Mohenjo-daro, and the lost-wax casting evidence in its structure.

cards.what: The largest Indus city by area is not Mohenjo-daro — it is Rakhigarhi, far to the east on the Ghaggar plain, still mostly unexcavated under and around a living village. The centre of gravity of the civilisation may be further east than the famous sites suggest.
cards.why: The biggest city is the least known one, and much of it is still under a village.
cards.evidence: The surface survey and limited excavation at Rakhigarhi, and its measured extent.

cards.what: A great brick basin at Lothal, beside a warehouse and a bead factory, connected by a channel toward the estuary. Read as a dockyard it is the world's oldest; read as a reservoir it is a very large water tank. The argument has run for sixty years on the same evidence.
cards.why: Either the oldest dock on earth or a water tank. The evidence permits both, and the game says so.
cards.evidence: The excavated basin, its inlet channel and spillway, and the sling stones and stone anchors found in it.
cards.dispute: Tidal calculations, the channel's dimensions and the salt crust are marshalled on both sides. Marine archaeology has not settled it.

cards.match: Weight standards adopted in the Gulf
cards.what: Merchants in Dilmun and along the Gulf adopt the Indus weight system for their own transactions. It is one thing to export beads; it is another for foreign ports to keep your units. Standards travel further than the people who set them.
cards.why: The clearest sign of Indus commercial weight: other people adopted the weights.
cards.evidence: The Indus-standard weight sets excavated at Bahrain and the Gulf entrepôts.

cards.what: The direct run from the Indus to Sumer gives way to a staged trade through Dilmun, where cargoes change hands and Mesopotamian records log the traffic. Middlemen appear in the world's first long-distance maritime economy almost as soon as the economy itself.
cards.why: The entrepôt is as old as the trade. Somebody always sits in the middle.
cards.evidence: The Dilmun customs and trade records in cuneiform, and the Indus material excavated on Bahrain.

cards.what: A city on a salt-desert island, with no river and unreliable rain, cuts sixteen reservoirs into rock and builds check dams on two seasonal streams, storing a year's water. The reservoirs take up a tenth of the walled area. The city lasts fifteen hundred years.
cards.why: The driest Indus city lived longest, because it engineered its water like a state utility.
cards.evidence: The excavated reservoir system at Dholavira, its dams, and the occupation sequence.

cards.what: A stalagmite in a Meghalaya cave records the 4.2 kiloyear drought so clearly that geologists name the current age of the earth after it: the Meghalayan. The formal marker for the epoch every human alive inhabits is a drought signature in an Indian cave.
cards.why: The geological present is officially defined by the drought that ended the Indus cities.
cards.evidence: The Mawmluh speleothem record, adopted by the International Commission on Stratigraphy in 2018.

cards.what: The ships stop being mentioned. The word Meluhha survives in later texts but drifts — eventually it means somewhere in Africa. A trading partner of six centuries fades out of the ledgers of the only people writing ledgers.
cards.why: The Indus decline, observed from the outside, as an entry that stops appearing.
cards.evidence: The cuneiform record: dense Meluhha references in the Akkadian and Ur III periods, then silence.

cards.what: Caches of massive copper objects turn up across the Ganga-Yamuna doab: harpoons, swords with antenna hilts, and flat anthropomorphic figures like spread-eagled men. They are heavy, unwieldy, mostly unused, and buried in groups. Who made them and what they were for is unresolved.
cards.why: Hundreds of kilograms of worked copper, buried on purpose, by people we cannot name.
cards.evidence: The hoards themselves, associated loosely with Ochre Coloured Pottery, from dozens of doab findspots.
cards.dispute: Ritual deposits, ingot wealth, weapons of a vanished people and trade stock have all been argued. The association with any one culture is loose.

cards.what: One site on the Kachi plain holds horse and camel bones, rice and millet, all together in the centuries after the cities. Pirak is what the post-urban world looks like when it works: new animals, new crops, smaller settlements, wider connections.
cards.why: The world after the cities is not a ruin. It is a reorganisation, and Pirak is its type site.
cards.evidence: The Pirak excavation sequence, its faunal and botanical record, and its terracotta horse-and-rider figurines.

cards.what: Four bronzes from a Deccan village hoard: a chariot with driver and team, an elephant, a rhinoceros, a buffalo, all on wheels or axles, together weighing over sixty kilograms. They are the largest bronzes of Indian prehistory, found far south of anywhere that was supposed to be casting like this.
cards.why: Sixty kilograms of bronze sculpture from a place the metallurgical map said could not produce it.
cards.evidence: The hoard itself, now in Mumbai, and the Daimabad site sequence.
cards.dispute: The date is argued across nearly a millennium, from late Harappan to the historic period, largely because hoards carry no stratigraphy.

cards.what: The solid cart wheel is heavy and slow. The spoked wheel is light enough to make a vehicle fast — which changes what a vehicle is for, from carrying grain to carrying warriors. The chariot follows it into the record, and into the hymns.
cards.why: A carpentry innovation with military consequences. Speed enters the battlefield.
cards.evidence: Spoked-wheel depictions and models from the second millennium, and the chariotry of the Vedic corpus.

cards.what: Across the peninsula, communities begin marking their dead with stone: cists, dolmens, urn fields, stone circles. The burials carry iron almost from the start, and the monuments organise the landscape for a thousand years — visible claims by the dead on behalf of the living.
cards.why: The south's iron age announces itself in graves, and the graves are property markers as much as memorials.
cards.evidence: The megalithic cemeteries from the Deccan to the far south, with their iron grave goods and dating.

cards.match: Iron working begins in the Ganga plain
cards.what: Iron ore is nearly everywhere, unlike copper and tin. When smiths in the Ganga plain learn to smelt and forge it, metal tools stop being an elite good and become an agricultural one. The axe and the ploughshare follow, and then the forest recedes.
cards.why: The democratising metal: cheap enough for farmers, and the eastern forests fall to it.
cards.evidence: Iron slag and artefacts from Malhar, Raja Nala ka Tila and the PGW settlements, with their radiocarbon dates.
cards.dispute: Dates for the earliest Gangetic iron have moved steadily earlier and are still argued, as is whether the southern iron tradition is older and separate.

cards.match: The knowledge economy runs entirely on memory
cards.what: There is no script anywhere on the subcontinent. Everything known — ritual, genealogy, boundary, medicine, story — exists only in living heads and dies with them unless taught. The entire apparatus this game simulates is, at this moment, people.
cards.why: The purest form of the game's central problem: a civilisation's knowledge with no storage medium but its members.
cards.evidence: The absence of writing between the Indus script's end and Brahmi, roughly sixteen centuries.

cards.what: Some hymns end with verses praising the patron who paid for the performance: so many cows, so many horses, gold, chariots, women. They are receipts in verse, and they are the earliest surviving record of the knowledge economy actually transacting.
cards.why: The oldest invoices in Indian literature, embedded in scripture.
cards.evidence: The dana-stuti passages of the Rigveda, with their itemised gifts.

cards.match: The iron axe opens the eastern forest
cards.what: The middle and lower Ganga plain is under forest that stone and copper tools cannot economically clear. Iron axes can. Settlement moves east along the river for three centuries, burning and cutting, and the rice land that results will feed every empire in the game.
cards.why: The clearance that creates the subcontinent's centre of gravity. Magadha is downstream of the axe.
cards.evidence: The eastward march of PGW and then NBPW settlement, and the charcoal and pollen records of clearance.

cards.what: A consecrated horse wanders for a year, escorted by warriors; where it walks unchallenged, the king's writ runs. Then it is brought home and sacrificed in a rite that takes a year to perform. Sovereignty is being defined as the ability to protect a horse across other people's land.
cards.why: Kingship performed as ritual theatre, with the border decided by where anyone dares stop the horse.
cards.evidence: The shrauta descriptions of the rite, and the later inscriptions of kings who claim to have performed it.

cards.what: Two tribes merge, the ritual system is codified around their court, and the hymn collections are arranged. Something new appears: an entity that outlives its chief, taxes rather than raids, and sponsors the fixing of texts. The first state of the Ganga plain assembles itself around a liturgy.
cards.why: The state and the canon are born in the same project, each stabilising the other.
cards.evidence: The Kuru realm of the later Vedic texts, read against the PGW settlement record of the Doab.

cards.what: The hymns are organised: family books in the middle, framed by later collections, ordered within books by deity and metre. Arrangement is a technology — a fixed sequence is checkable, teachable and hard to corrupt. The canon becomes a structure rather than a heap.
cards.why: An oral text acquires an architecture, and the architecture is what preserves it.
cards.evidence: The collection's structure itself, whose internal ordering rules are visible and consistent.

cards.what: Nearly every verse of the Samaveda is taken from the Rigveda; what is new is the music. The verses are set to fixed melodies, stretched and ornamented for singing at the soma rite. It is the oldest continuously transmitted music in the world.
cards.why: A remix, formally — and the beginning of Indian music's documented history.
cards.evidence: The Samaveda's overlap with the Rigveda, and the living saman chant traditions.

cards.what: The fourth collection is the household's: healing charms, love spells, curses, rites for building a house and calming a quarrel, herbs named with their uses. It is the closest the Vedic corpus comes to ordinary life, which is why the priestly tradition was long uneasy about it.
cards.why: The Veda of everyday trouble — medicine, marriage and malice — and the ancestor of Ayurveda's claim to Vedic standing.
cards.evidence: The Shaunaka and Paippalada recensions, the latter recovered largely from Odisha palm leaf.

cards.what: The corpus is now too large for any one lineage to hold, so it divides: schools of transmission, each responsible for one recension of one Veda, each with its own accent rules and ancillary texts. It is redundancy by specialisation — and every school that later dies takes its recension with it.
cards.why: The corpus is sharded across institutions. Most of the shards will not survive.
cards.evidence: The named shakhas of the tradition, the handful still recited, and the many known only as titles.

cards.what: Instead of broadcasting seed, cultivators raise seedlings in a nursery bed and transplant them into flooded fields. The labour is brutal and the yield increase is transformative. Wet rice becomes the most productive agriculture on the subcontinent, and the plain that masters it becomes its centre.
cards.why: The technique that makes the eastern Ganga plain the richest place in the game.
cards.evidence: The agronomy of the shift, and the settlement intensification of the middle Ganga in the same centuries.

cards.what: The village becomes a unit that can be assessed: so many households, so much land, owing so much. Tribute hardens from gift toward obligation. Every state in the rest of this game stands on this change, and the texts record the resentment it caused.
cards.why: Taxation is invented, and it is invented on the village.
cards.evidence: The later Vedic terminology of bali and bhaga hardening, and the Brahmana passages on the eater and the eaten.

cards.what: A city on the Yamuna raises an earthen rampart faced with brick, kilometres around, with gates and towers. Nothing on this scale has been built since the Indus cities. Urban life is returning, and it returns armed.
cards.why: The second urbanisation's first great wall — cities are back, and they expect trouble.
cards.evidence: The excavated defences at Kausambi and their dating.
cards.dispute: The rampart's earliest date is a long-running argument, with proposals differing by several centuries.

cards.what: A luxury ceramic with a mirror-black surface appears in the middle Ganga and spreads along the trade routes until sherds of it turn up from Taxila to Sri Lanka. Where NBPW goes, urbanism and long-distance exchange have gone. It is the index fossil of the second urbanisation.
cards.why: A dinner service maps the return of cities.
cards.evidence: The NBPW distribution and its find contexts across the subcontinent.

cards.what: As clearance and settlement expand, the people of the forest — hunters, shifting cultivators, herders — stop being everyone's neighbours and become a category: those beyond the boundary. The texts begin naming them as other. The frontier of this game is not a border on the west; it is the treeline everywhere.
cards.why: The longest-running conflict in the game begins, and it is not between kingdoms.
cards.evidence: The later Vedic and epic vocabulary for forest peoples, and the archaeology of settlement expansion.

cards.what: Craft associations acquire standing: potters, weavers, metalworkers, caravan traders organised in bodies that set standards, train apprentices, adjudicate disputes and speak for the trade. Kings deal with them as entities. They will shortly begin taking deposits.
cards.why: Organised labour and organised capital arrive together, in the same institution.
cards.evidence: The shreni references across the Pali canon, the epics and the Arthashastra, and the later guild inscriptions.

cards.what: Silver circulates in bent bars of standard weight, cut and checked. They are not quite coins — no authority stamps them — but they are money in everything but the stamp: a medium, a standard, a store. The stamp arrives within a century.
cards.why: Money is being assembled piece by piece, and weight comes before sovereignty.
cards.evidence: The bent-bar silver from Taxila-area hoards and its weight standards.

cards.what: The word for a people acquires a suffix and becomes the word for a territory: jana, the tribe, becomes janapada, where the tribe has set its foot. Identity attaches to land rather than kin. Every border in the rest of the game descends from this change in grammar.
cards.why: The map is invented — in language, before it is drawn anywhere.
cards.evidence: The terminological shift traced across the later Vedic and early Buddhist texts.

cards.what: Vardhamana, called Mahavira, systematises a tradition he did not begin — Jains count him twenty-fourth of their teachers — around non-violence carried to its full consequence: toward animals, insects, and in the limit toward the self. The order he leaves is small, disciplined, and it never afterwards disappears.
cards.why: The most rigorous ethical position in the ancient world, and the oldest surviving renouncer order.
cards.evidence: The Jain Agamas and the shared testimony of the Buddhist canon, where Mahavira appears as a rival.
cards.dispute: His dates track the Buddha's, and both chronologies are argued within a century.

cards.what: Vajji, Malla, the Shakyas and others are governed not by kings but by assemblies of heads of families — meeting in halls, deliberating, voting. The Buddha, born in one, later names the Vajji assembly's habits as the model for his own order's procedure.
cards.why: The republic is an Indian political form, and the monastic sangha is partly its heir.
cards.evidence: The Pali canon's descriptions of gana-sangha procedure, and the Mahaparinibbana Sutta's seven conditions.

cards.match: Taxila becomes a centre of learning
cards.what: Students travel to the northwest to study — medicine, archery, grammar, ritual — under named teachers, paying at the end, living in the teacher's house. There is no campus and no institution: Taxila is a city where teachers live, which is what a university is before anyone builds one.
cards.why: Higher education exists as a market of teachers three centuries before anyone endows a building for it.
cards.evidence: The Jataka references to students sent to Takkasila, and the excavated city itself.

cards.what: Two great routes are named: the northern road from the Gangetic capitals to the northwest, and the southern road into the Deccan. Caravans move along them with escorts, stages and ferries. The game's trade network has a trunk from here on, and every empire will try to hold both roads.
cards.why: The subcontinent acquires its permanent economic axes.
cards.evidence: The route references across the Pali canon and the grammarians, and the alignment of early urban sites.

cards.what: Gosala teaches that everything is fixed: the soul migrates through a determined series of lives, and effort changes nothing. It draws followers for a thousand years, kings among their donors, and then vanishes so completely that its texts survive only as quotations in the polemics of its enemies.
cards.why: A major religion of ancient India, known entirely through people who despised it.
cards.evidence: The Samannaphala Sutta and Jain sources, both hostile, and the Barabar cave dedications.

cards.what: The Buddha's followers are organised as a corporate body with rules of admission, procedure and expulsion. Property is held by the order, not the man. When the founder dies, the institution does not — which is precisely what it was designed for.
cards.why: The corporation that outlives its founder is invented here, and every endowment in this game imitates it.
cards.evidence: The Vinaya's constitutional machinery, and the order's demonstrated survival of its founder by twenty-five centuries.

cards.what: A fort at the confluence of the Ganga and the Son, placed to control river traffic, grows within two centuries into the largest city in the world. The Buddha, passing the construction site in the tradition, remarks that greatness and ruin will both come to it from flood, fire and quarrel.
cards.why: The capital of the next four empires is founded as a customs post.
cards.evidence: The Pali account of the fort's construction, and the excavated palisade and palace remains.

cards.what: The order meets in the rains after the founder's death and recites everything: Ananda the discourses, Upali the discipline. What is confirmed by the assembly is canon. It is a memory institution acting deliberately to fix its holdings, and it works — for the next four centuries the canon is carried this way.
cards.why: A library commits itself to collective memory, on purpose, by vote.
cards.evidence: The Vinaya's own account of the Rajagriha council, and the canon's demonstrated oral coherence.

cards.what: The guilds begin taking deposits and paying interest, and endowments learn to use them: donate a principal to a guild, and the interest feeds a monk or lights a lamp in perpetuity. The instrument is so stable that inscriptions record endowments running for centuries.
cards.why: The perpetual endowment is engineered, and knowledge acquires an income.
cards.evidence: The Nasik and Karle cave inscriptions recording deposits with weavers' guilds at stated rates of interest.

cards.what: The punch-marked silver standardises across the northern kingdoms into the karshapana, and Magadha's issues gradually crowd out the rest. Whoever's coin the market prefers collects a quiet tax on everyone who uses it.
cards.why: Monetary consolidation precedes political consolidation, and predicts it.
cards.evidence: The hoard evidence showing Magadhan series dominating circulation before the Mauryan unification.

cards.what: A century on, monks of Vaishali are accepting gold and silver, and the order splits over whether they may. The council rules against, the losers walk out with the majority, and the first schism is on the books — over ten small rules, of which money is one.
cards.why: Institutions do not usually split over doctrine. They split over money and discipline, and this one did.
cards.evidence: The Vinaya accounts of the Vaishali council from both descendant traditions.

cards.what: Clerks adapt the Aramaic they learned under Persian administration into a script for local speech, written right to left. For seven centuries the northwest writes in it, and then it dies with the trade routes that carried it — leaving Brahmi's descendants the whole field.
cards.why: The subcontinent's other script: born of an empire's paperwork, dead with a trade network.
cards.evidence: The Kharoshthi corpus from the Ashokan edicts to the Central Asian documents.

cards.what: The tradition makes Chandragupta's rise the work of his minister, and hangs on that name the Arthashastra: a manual of state that discusses revenue, espionage, law, war and administration with a candour later ages found alarming. Whoever wrote it, somebody governed like this.
cards.why: Statecraft as a technical subject with a textbook, stripped of piety.
cards.evidence: The Arthashastra text and its parallels with Megasthenes and the Ashokan administrative record.
cards.dispute: The text's date is argued across five centuries, and its attribution to Chandragupta's minister is traditional rather than demonstrated.
