cards.what: The state enumerates its income: land revenue by class of soil, mines, salt, forests, herds, tolls, fines, and monopolies where monopoly pays. Officers assess, collectors collect, auditors audit the collectors. The Arthashastra's longest discussions are not about war. They are about revenue.
cards.why: Empire is an accounting achievement before it is a military one.
cards.evidence: The Arthashastra's revenue chapters, corroborated by the relief-order inscriptions at Sohgaura and Mahasthan.

cards.what: Two inscriptions — a copper plaque at Sohgaura, a limestone slab at Mahasthan — order the release of grain from state storehouses against famine, and provide for restocking after. They are administrative documents, not proclamations: the machinery assumes famines recur and stores against them.
cards.why: The state's oldest surviving documents in India are disaster-relief orders.
cards.evidence: The Sohgaura and Mahasthan inscriptions, both pre-Ashokan in script.

cards.what: A dam and reservoir are built at Girnar under Chandragupta's governor, and maintained: an inscription four centuries later records its repair after a storm, and another, three centuries after that, records repair again. The same waterwork is kept running by three successive polities across seven hundred years.
cards.why: Infrastructure maintained across dynasties — the least glamorous and most impressive fact in the record.
cards.evidence: The Junagadh rock: Rudradaman's inscription of 150 CE and Skandagupta's of 456, both recording repairs.

cards.what: The edict counts the Kalinga dead, states the king's remorse, and then defines the only conquest worth having as conquest by dhamma — and reports, as its evidence, missions sent to five named Greek kings. It also warns the forest peoples that the king's patience, though real, has limits.
cards.why: The document is subtler than its reputation: remorse, propaganda and threat in one text.
cards.evidence: Rock Edict XIII at Girnar, Kalsi and Shahbazgarhi, with its named Hellenistic rulers fixing the chronology.

cards.what: A new cadre of officers is created to supervise moral welfare: of prisoners, of the aged, of religious communities including rivals. The state takes ethics into its administrative structure, with inspectors. Nothing quite like it exists anywhere else in the ancient world.
cards.why: A ministry of conscience, invented by the ruler who had the most to have a conscience about.
cards.evidence: The edicts instituting the dhamma-mahamattas and describing their remit.

cards.what: Under Ashoka's patronage the order purges itself of those judged to have entered for the endowments, fixes its texts, and — decisively — resolves to send missions outward: to Sri Lanka, to the northwest, to the Hellenistic west, to the Himalaya, to Suvarnabhumi.
cards.why: The decision to export. Everything about where Buddhism lives today follows from it.
cards.evidence: The Sri Lankan chronicle accounts, the schism edict, and the relic caskets at Sanchi naming Himalayan missionaries.

cards.what: A stupa is raised on a hill above Vidisha, and around it over centuries accrete railings, gateways and inscriptions — over six hundred of them, recording donations not from kings but from monks, nuns, merchants, and villagers, each named, many with their town.
cards.why: The great monument of early Buddhism was crowd-funded, and the donor list is carved on it.
cards.evidence: The Sanchi complex and its donative inscription corpus.

cards.what: The pillar inscriptions stop. Within fifty years the empire has contracted to its core and a general ends the dynasty at a military review. What was held together by an administration and a personality proves not to survive the second, and the first goes with it.
cards.why: The first pan-Indian state lasts one long lifetime past its builder. The game should make the player feel why.
cards.evidence: The end of the edict series, the Puranic king lists, and the numismatic record of contraction.

cards.what: The last Maurya is killed by his own commander-in-chief while inspecting the army — the Indian textbook case of the guardian problem the Arthashastra itself had warned about. The successor state is regional, brahmanical in patronage, and the subcontinent returns to a system of competing kingdoms.
cards.why: Empires end administratively before they end militarily. The coup is a formality.
cards.evidence: The Puranic accounts and Bana's later retelling, with the Shunga patronage record at Bharhut and Sanchi.

cards.match: A generation of palm leaf reaches the end
cards.what: Palm leaf lasts about three centuries in Indian conditions, less in the wet ones. Every written work is therefore on a clock: recopied within its window or gone. From here to the arrival of paper, the corpus survives only at the speed scribes work.
cards.why: The material itself imposes the recopying treadmill the whole knowledge economy runs on.
cards.evidence: The survival profile of the manuscript record: almost nothing physical survives from before the second millennium CE, however old the text.

cards.what: The Tamil country resolves into three lines — Chera, Chola, Pandya — each with a crest, a garland and a river, plus chieftains between them. The arrangement is already old when Ashoka's edicts name all three as neighbours beyond the border.
cards.why: A political geography stable enough to outlast every empire to the north of it.
cards.evidence: The Ashokan rock edicts naming the three, and the Sangam corpus built around them.

cards.what: An Indo-Greek king questions a Buddhist monk, and the exchange becomes a book: the Questions of Milinda, in Pali, with the king pressing genuinely Greek objections and the monk answering with the chariot dismantled part by part. Menander's coins are the commonest of any Indo-Greek king.
cards.why: A Greek king inside the Pali canon's orbit — the clearest single artefact of the meeting of two worlds.
cards.evidence: The Milindapanha itself, and Menander's abundant coinage from the Punjab to the Kabul valley.

cards.what: The Great Commentary on Panini — argumentative, digressive, full of asides about how people actually speak, what words villagers use, and a mention of a recent Greek siege. Grammar is being done as a live science, and the asides are now historians' evidence.
cards.why: The best granary of incidental fact in ancient India is a grammar commentary's digressions.
cards.evidence: The Mahabhashya, with its yavana references fixing its date to the Shunga period.

cards.what: A Greek ambassador from Taxila, Heliodorus son of Dion, raises a Garuda column to Vasudeva at Besnagar and says on it that he is a Bhagavata — a devotee. A Greek official, in an Indian court, publicly professing an Indian devotional faith, in stone.
cards.why: Assimilation is not a modern idea. The envoy converted, and told everybody.
cards.evidence: The pillar itself, still standing at Vidisha, with its Prakrit inscription.

cards.what: Prayer halls and monasteries are cut into the ghats above the trade routes, and the inscriptions say who paid: guilds, caravan traders, bankers, a perfumer, a ploughman, individual monks and nuns. The great architecture of the age is subscription-funded infrastructure on the trade roads.
cards.why: Religion, commerce and civil engineering in one institution — cut where the caravans actually passed.
cards.evidence: The Karle, Bhaja, Junnar and Kanheri complexes and their donative inscriptions.

cards.what: Over six hundred short inscriptions on Sanchi's railings and gateways name ordinary donors — monks, nuns, weavers, ivory carvers of a named town — each paying for a crossbar or a panel. Some of the biggest names are women.
cards.why: The monument as a ledger: early Indian religion crowd-funded, and it published the donor list.
cards.evidence: The Sanchi inscription corpus, including the guild of ivory workers of Vidisha signing a gateway panel.

cards.what: Tradition credits Karikala with a low dam of unhewn stone across the Kaveri where it splits — the Kallanai. Raised and recased over centuries, it still functions in the modern irrigation system: dated to antiquity, engineering in continuous use.
cards.why: Possibly the oldest water-regulating structure on earth still doing its job.
cards.evidence: The structure itself, its later inscriptions and recasings, and the Sangam references to Karikala's works.
cards.dispute: Karikala's dates and deeds are legend-encrusted; the dam's original form and date are argued even while the water goes on obeying it.

cards.what: A Deccan dynasty knits the peninsula's trade together: west-coast ports through the ghat passes to inland markets, and across to the east coast. Their coins are everywhere along the routes, and their queens' names appear in the royal titles — Gautamiputra, son of Gautami.
cards.why: The Deccan stops being between north and south, and becomes a power because it is between.
cards.evidence: The Satavahana coin distribution, the Naneghat and Nasik inscriptions, and the matronymic royal style.

cards.what: Into the epic's sixth book, on the morning of the battle, a dialogue is inserted: a warrior refuses to fight his kin, and his charioteer answers him through every school of argument available — duty, knowledge, discipline, devotion — before the reveal. The insertion becomes the most read text in the tradition.
cards.why: Seven hundred verses of philosophy placed at the exact point of maximum narrative pressure.
cards.evidence: The Gita's position in the Bhishma Parva, and the layering visible in its language and doctrine.

cards.what: A treatise codifies theatre whole: stagecraft, gesture, metre, costume, music, and the theory of rasa — that art works by evoking flavours of feeling in the audience, not by depicting them. Every classical performance tradition in India descends from arguing with this book.
cards.why: The oldest surviving theory of aesthetics anywhere, and it is a working stage manual.
cards.evidence: The text and Abhinavagupta's commentary, without which much of it would be unreadable.

cards.what: A settlement on the Coromandel coast starts filling with Mediterranean material: wine amphorae, Arretine tableware stamped by Italian potters, Roman lamps and glass. Somebody is buying, and the muslin and beads made on site say what they were selling.
cards.why: The Roman trade touches ground level: a village turned entrepot, visible sherd by sherd.
cards.evidence: Wheeler's and later excavations at Arikamedu, with the stamped Arretine ware fixing the chronology.

cards.what: Pliny complains that India drains fifty million sesterces from Rome every year, for pepper and luxuries. Hoards of Roman gold and silver coins across south India confirm the direction of flow. The empire's moralists call it ruinous; the ships keep sailing.
cards.why: A trade imbalance argued about in the Roman senate and buried in Kerala hoards.
cards.evidence: Pliny's complaint, the Coimbatore-region coin hoards, and the Muziris papyrus's cargo values.

cards.what: A confederation out of Central Asia takes the northwest and builds a state that faces both ways: summer capital toward Bactria, winter capital at Mathura, coins in Greek script naming Iranian, Greek and Indian gods. Under their peace, the Silk Road and the Ganga plain do business.
cards.why: The invasion that became an era: patrons of the first Buddha images and the road to China.
cards.evidence: The Rabatak inscription, the two capitals, and the syncretic coinage.
cards.becomes: The Gandharan and Mathura workshops, the Fourth Council, and Buddhism's transmission into the Tarim and China.

cards.what: The Saka rulers of the west do something no Indian dynasty had: they put the date on the money, year by year, in the Shaka era. For three centuries their silver gives a dated sequence historians can hang everything else on.
cards.why: The most precisely dated coin series in ancient India, and the era on it is still official.
cards.evidence: The Kshatrapa silver series with regnal and era dates, and the Shaka era's survival as India's national calendar.

cards.what: Kanishka's accession founds an era. Which year that was — 78, 127, or something else — has consumed a century of scholarship, because half of Central Asian chronology hangs on it. The era of 78 becomes the Shaka era, later adopted as the Indian national calendar.
cards.why: One missing date, and the chronology of two regions wobbles around it.
cards.evidence: The Rabatak and other Kanishka-era inscriptions, and the long argument over the era's epoch.
cards.dispute: 78 CE and 127 CE both retain serious support; the game uses a window rather than an assertion.

cards.what: Under Kanishka a council meets in Kashmir — the tradition says to fix the Sarvastivada commentaries. Around the same decades, sutras of a new kind circulate: the Mahayana, with its bodhisattva ideal. The religion is reorganising itself at both ends, canon and vision.
cards.why: Buddhism's second great turn happens under an invader's patronage, on the frontier.
cards.evidence: Xuanzang's account of the council, and the earliest Chinese translations dating Mahayana circulation.
cards.dispute: The council's historicity outside the northern tradition, and the Mahayana's origins, are both substantially argued.

cards.what: While Gandhara sculpts the Buddha in Hellenistic drapery, Mathura develops its own answer in red sandstone: broad-shouldered, open-eyed, Indian in every convention. Two solutions to the same new problem, arrived at simultaneously, seven hundred kilometres apart.
cards.why: The image of the Buddha has two independent birthplaces, and the game should show both.
cards.evidence: The dated Mathura and Gandhara corpora, and the argument over priority which the dates leave open.

cards.what: One king's coins carry Herakles and Buddha, Mithra and Shiva, Nanaia and the Greek sun god — the pantheon of everyone in his empire, each labelled in Bactrian script. It is not confusion. It is policy for a state whose subjects pray in five directions.
cards.why: Religious pluralism as minting policy, eighteen centuries before anyone called it that.
cards.evidence: The Kushan coin corpus with its labelled deities.

cards.what: A Buddhist monk writes the Buddha's life as a court epic in polished Sanskrit — the language of the tradition his subject walked away from. Half survives in Sanskrit; the whole survives in Tibetan and Chinese, which is the corpus mechanic in one book.
cards.why: Sanskrit kavya's first great poem is Buddhist, and most of it survives only in translation.
cards.evidence: The Sanskrit fragments and the complete Tibetan and Chinese versions.

cards.what: The Saka ruler Rudradaman repairs the Sudarshana dam after a storm and records it — in ornate Sanskrit prose, the first long inscription in the language. He boasts that he repaired it without oppressive taxes or forced labour, which tells you what usually happened.
cards.why: Sanskrit enters the inscriptional record as a boast about disaster relief done fairly.
cards.evidence: The Junagadh rock inscription of 150 CE.

cards.what: A Tamil epic in which the hero is executed on a false charge and his widow Kannagi proves the injustice before the Pandya king, whose heart stops from shame — after which she burns Madurai with her own grief. The state's failure, not the enemy's, is the tragedy.
cards.why: An epic where the moral catastrophe is a miscarriage of justice, and the avenger is a widow.
cards.evidence: The Silappatikaram text, and the Kannagi cult attested across the Tamil country and Sri Lanka.

cards.what: The Sangam corpus is fixed: eight anthologies and ten long songs, 2,381 poems, 473 named poets. The love poems never name their speakers; the war poems name everyone. A complete literature with its own conventions, owing nothing to Sanskrit models.
cards.why: A second classical literature, complete and independent, in a different language family.
cards.evidence: The anthologies with their colophons, and the poetics of the Tolkappiyam that they obey.

cards.what: Nagarjuna argues that nothing possesses independent existence — not objects, not the self, not nirvana, not the argument itself — and that this emptiness is not nihilism but the condition of anything happening at all. Every later Buddhist philosophy positions itself relative to him.
cards.why: The most consequential philosopher between the Buddha and Shankara, and the hinge both traditions turn on.
cards.evidence: The Mulamadhyamakakarika and its unbroken commentarial traditions in Sanskrit, Tibetan and Chinese.

cards.what: Animal fables framed as a crash course in statecraft for three dull princes: alliances, betrayals, the mouse that frees the doves. It will be translated into Pahlavi, then Arabic, then across Europe, becoming one of the most travelled books in world history.
cards.why: India's most successful export before the numerals, and it is a book of talking animals about power.
cards.evidence: The Sanskrit recensions and the translation chain through Kalila wa-Dimna into forty languages.

cards.what: A Magadhan family marries into the old Licchavi prestige, and within two generations Samudragupta has built the largest state since the Mauryas — but run differently: defeated kings reinstated as tributaries, the mandala worked rather than the province annexed.
cards.why: The classical empire: lighter-handed than the Mauryan, and its cultural weather lasts far longer.
cards.evidence: The Allahabad pillar inscription, the Gupta coin series, and the era of 320 that dates the age.

cards.what: On an Ashokan pillar, Samudragupta's court poet lists the campaigns: kings of the north uprooted and their lands annexed; kings of the south captured and released to rule as tributaries; frontier peoples paying tribute. It is the mandala system stated as autobiography.
cards.why: Graded sovereignty in the king's own record — the game's sovereignty model, written in 350.
cards.evidence: The Allahabad pillar prashasti of Harishena.

cards.what: Villages are granted to learned brahmins, revenue and all, in perpetuity. The grant deed specifies the scholars, sometimes the subjects. It is an endowment mechanism: the state converts revenue into a permanent teaching settlement that outlasts the dynasty that made it.
cards.why: Knowledge acquires a landed income, and the countryside acquires its universities.
cards.evidence: The copper-plate agrahara grants, thousands of them, naming grantees and their Vedic schools.

cards.what: The court at Ujjain gathers the tradition's greatest poet. Kalidasa's Shakuntala, his Cloud Messenger, his dynasty epic — court poetry at a polish never surpassed in Sanskrit, patronised by a state at its own peak. When Goethe read Shakuntala in translation he wrote a quatrain about it.
cards.why: The high-water mark of court Sanskrit, and Europe's first intoxication with Indian literature.
cards.evidence: The plays and poems, the traditional association with Chandragupta II's court, and the 1791 Jones translation.

cards.what: A Chinese monk in his sixties walks to India for monastic rules, spends six years travelling and two copying texts, and writes a sober report: the roads are safe, the hospitals in Pataliputra are free, the candalas live outside the towns and strike a stick to warn of their approach.
cards.why: An outsider's audit of Gupta India, unsentimental in both directions.
cards.evidence: Faxian's Record of Buddhist Kingdoms, and the texts he carried back and translated.

cards.what: Seven metres of forge-welded iron, over six tonnes, raised as a Vishnu standard around 400 — and essentially unrusted sixteen centuries later, protected by a phosphorus-rich passive film modern metallurgy has analysed with respect. The inscription names a king, probably Chandragupta II.
cards.why: A metallurgical result that would be respectable today, standing in a courtyard since 400.
cards.evidence: The pillar itself in the Qutb complex, its Sanskrit inscription, and the corrosion studies on its surface film.

cards.what: A scholar comes from India to the Mahavihara, is set a test — expound the whole doctrine from two verses — and produces the Visuddhimagga. He then reorganises the old Sinhala commentaries into Pali, fixing how the Theravada reads its own canon ever after.
cards.why: The editor as historical force: one man's redaction becomes a whole tradition's lens.
cards.evidence: The Visuddhimagga and the commentaries, with the Mahavamsa's account of his arrival and test.

cards.what: In a river gorge, under Vakataka patronage, cave halls are cut and painted: the Jataka stories in continuous narrative, courts and forests, dark-skinned and light-skinned figures side by side, the great bodhisattva with the blue lotus. Then patronage stops and the gorge keeps the paintings safe for thirteen centuries.
cards.why: The largest surviving body of ancient Indian painting, preserved by abandonment.
cards.evidence: The caves themselves, the Harishena-period dedicatory inscriptions, and the 1819 rediscovery.

cards.what: Zinc boils below the temperature its ore smelts at, so it vaporises and is lost — unless you invert the problem. At Zawar, retorts are packed with ore, sealed, and heated upside down so the vapour condenses downward into collectors. Industrial-scale heaps of spent retorts survive.
cards.why: A chemical-engineering inversion Europe managed only in 1738 — and the heaps prove the scale.
cards.evidence: The Zawar retort mounds and furnaces, radiocarbon dated, and the metallurgical analyses of the residues.

cards.what: An encyclopaedia of everything a court might ask an expert: astronomy and astrology, weather signs, architecture, gemmology, perfume recipes, the interpretation of the twitching of limbs. Varahamihira compiles, compares his sources, and often says which he trusts.
cards.why: What a sixth-century court considered knowable, in one book, with source criticism.
cards.evidence: The Brihat Samhita, and its quotations from earlier authorities now lost.

cards.match: The temple as a landholding corporation
cards.what: Temples begin to hold land, collect its revenue, employ staff, lend at interest and keep accounts — a corporate person with perpetual life. The god is a legal minor; the trustees act for him; the institution outlives dynasties. The south's economy reorganises around it.
cards.why: The most durable economic institution in Indian history takes legal form.
cards.evidence: The temple grant and account inscriptions, and the later case law treating the deity as a juristic person.

cards.match: Harsha; the last great northern power
cards.what: A young king assembles the north for forty years by energy and alliance — moving court, personally administered, patron of Nalanda, host to Xuanzang, author of three plays. When he dies without an heir the assembly collapses, and the north does not reunite for five centuries.
cards.why: A state held together by one man's momentum, and the proof is what happens the day he stops.
cards.evidence: Bana's Harshacharita, Xuanzang's account, Harsha's own plays and grants.

cards.what: In one town on the Malaprabha, generations of masons build temple after temple in different plans — apsidal, flat-roofed, northern towered, southern tiered — as if working through the design space. The results stand a few hundred metres apart, drafts left standing.
cards.why: The laboratory where Indian temple architecture worked out what a temple is.
cards.evidence: The Aihole complex itself, with Pattadakal and Badami completing the sequence.

cards.what: One basalt scarp carries thirty-four excavations: Buddhist monasteries, Hindu temples, Jain shrines, cut over three centuries by overlapping patrons. Three religions sharing one cliff, one workforce, and largely one architectural language.
cards.why: Coexistence in the most durable medium available.
cards.evidence: The Ellora complex, its sequence and inscriptions.

cards.what: Bengal's first big king builds a state from Gauda, fights Harsha's family, and enters the record twice: in his own coins, and in the accounts of Buddhist enemies who accuse him of felling the Bodhi tree. The Bengali calendar is traditionally reckoned from his era.
cards.why: A regional power's founder, remembered almost entirely through hostile witnesses.
cards.evidence: Shashanka's coinage, Xuanzang's and the Manjushrimulakalpa's hostile accounts, and the Bengali era tradition.
cards.dispute: The Bodhi tree story comes only from his enemies, and the Bengali era's origin is argued.

cards.what: Xuanzang describes it from inside: thousands of students, a hundred lecture rooms a day, an examination at the gate most candidates fail, a library quarter with a nine-storeyed building. Admission is by debate, the endowment is a hundred villages, and the day is regulated by a water clock.
cards.why: The greatest school of the age, described by a foreign student who passed its entrance exam.
cards.evidence: Xuanzang's and Yijing's first-hand accounts, and the excavated campus.

cards.what: On a beach south of Madras the Pallavas begin carving: whole temples cut from granite boulders, a cliff face relief of the Ganges descending crowded with gods, elephants and ascetics, and rathas left unfinished at every stage of work.
cards.why: Stone carving at the scale of landscape, with the working method left visible.
cards.evidence: The Mahabalipuram monuments, and the Pallava inscriptions across them.

cards.what: A treatise on how poetry works — ornament, style, the ten qualities — written with such clarity that it is translated and becomes the foundational poetics of Tibet, and shapes literary theory in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.
cards.why: Indian literary criticism becomes an export discipline.
cards.evidence: The Kavyadarsha and its Tibetan and Sinhala adaptations.

cards.match: Bhakti moves along the pilgrimage roads
cards.what: The Tamil saints do not write for readers; they sing at temples, and they walk between them. The corpus organises itself as an itinerary — hymns keyed to shrines — and devotion spreads at walking pace along the roads that link them.
cards.why: Knowledge distributed by pilgrimage: the network is the medium.
cards.evidence: The Tevaram and Divya Prabandham's shrine-by-shrine structure, and the padal petra sthalams.

cards.what: After a period the sources call matsyanyaya — the justice of fishes, big eating small — the notables of Bengal choose a king. Gopala is elected. The dynasty he founds rules for four centuries and funds the great monasteries; its origin story is an agreement to stop the anarchy.
cards.why: A major dynasty that dates itself from an election, remembered as the end of the big fish.
cards.evidence: The Khalimpur plate of Dharmapala describing his father's election, and the Pala grant series.

cards.what: Workers start at the top of the cliff and remove everything that is not a temple: courtyard, gateway, life-size elephants, a two-storey shrine, all one piece of mountain. An estimated two hundred thousand tonnes of basalt are taken away. Nothing is built; everything is revealed by subtraction.
cards.why: The largest monolithic structure on earth, made entirely by removal.
cards.evidence: The Kailasa itself, and the Rashtrakuta grant recording royal astonishment at it.

cards.what: At the new Abbasid capital, an Indian embassy's astronomical texts are turned into the Zij al-Sindhind. With the astronomy travel the numerals and the zero. Arabic science's first foundation course is Indian, before the Greek translations arrive.
cards.why: Baghdad learns to calculate the Indian way first — and teaches Europe later.
cards.evidence: The Arabic bibliographers' accounts of the embassy and translation, and the numeral forms' transmission.

cards.what: The monastery-college with an endowed seat and a rule of succession: each head names the line forward, the institution holds the property, and the founder's teaching becomes a chair rather than a memory. Shankara's four are the model; every sect builds its own.
cards.why: The technology for making a school of thought immortal.
cards.evidence: The matha traditions, their succession lists and endowment records.

cards.match: Sri Lankan monks carry the canon
cards.what: From the island the Pali canon travels east: to the Mon country, to Burma, later to Siam and Cambodia and Laos. The transmission is monastic and textual, and it makes Sri Lanka — not India — the reference point for Southeast Asian Buddhism ever after.
cards.why: The redundancy strategy pays out at continental scale: the copy becomes the source.
cards.evidence: The Southeast Asian ordination and textual lineages tracing themselves to the Mahavihara.

cards.what: A minister leaves the Pandya court after an encounter he describes as being seized by god, and writes hymns whose emotional register — abasement, longing, ecstasy — sets the tone for Tamil Shaiva devotion. The tradition says his Tiruvasagam melts even stone hearts.
cards.why: The confessional voice enters Tamil religion, first person and unguarded.
cards.evidence: The Tiruvasagam corpus and its liturgical use in Shaiva temples since.

cards.what: The Krishna narrative is given its fullest telling — the child-god, the cowherd women, the disc-bearing king — in a Sanskrit deliberately archaised to sound Vedic. It becomes the single most influential devotional text in India, seeding movements from Bengal to the Gujarat coast.
cards.why: The book behind half the bhakti movements of the next millennium.
cards.evidence: The text, its southern origins argued from internal evidence, and its commentarial and performance traditions.

cards.what: The eastern monasteries develop a refined bronze and manuscript-painting tradition: gilded deities, palm-leaf covers painted in miniature. Carried by monks and traders, the style becomes the direct model for the art of Tibet, Nepal and much of Southeast Asia.
cards.why: The last great Buddhist art of India, and the template for the Himalayan art that outlived it.
cards.evidence: The Pala bronzes and illuminated manuscripts, and their Tibetan and Nepalese descendants.

cards.what: The Chola countryside runs on two parallel systems: the nadu, an assembly of cultivating villages, and the brahmadeya, the endowed brahmin settlement with its own assembly. Both keep records, both manage water, and the state deals with each on its own terms.
cards.why: Local government as the Cholas actually ran it — plural, chartered, and documented.
cards.evidence: The Chola inscription corpus distinguishing ur, sabha and nadu assemblies and their procedures.

cards.what: Sales, mortgages, endowments, tax settlements — the south's economic life starts being cut into temple walls at scale, because stone at a sacred site is the safest registry available. Tens of thousands of inscriptions accumulate. The temples become the archive of the economy.
cards.why: Pre-modern India's densest economic record exists because walls were the safest database.
cards.evidence: The South Indian inscription corpus, the largest body of pre-modern economic documents in the subcontinent.

cards.what: A widowed Chola queen spends five decades rebuilding brick temples in stone, endowing lamps, gilding, and recording every gift with her name and titles. Her patronage fixes the early Chola temple style, and her portrait bronze was worshipped after her death.
cards.why: Institutional patronage as a woman's career, documented in her own inscriptions for fifty years.
cards.evidence: The inscription series naming her across a dozen temples, and the Konerirajapuram bronzes.

cards.what: Uttaramerur's inscriptions specify committees — for tanks, gardens, gold, justice, famine — chosen annually by lot from qualified households. Service is unpaid, accounts are audited, and defaulters and their relatives are barred from standing.
cards.why: Administration by rotating committee, with conflict-of-interest rules, in the tenth century.
cards.evidence: The Uttaramerur constitutional inscriptions and parallel committee records at other sites.

cards.what: Endowment capital does not sit idle: temples lend it to village assemblies at stated interest, and the interest funds the lamp, the offering, the reciter. The inscriptions record principal, rate and purpose. The temple functions as the countryside's bank.
cards.why: The endowment becomes a credit system, and the sacred and fiscal economies merge.
cards.evidence: Chola-period loan inscriptions recording deposits with assemblies at specified rates.

cards.what: Rajaraja has the land measured and classified — wet, dry, garden, waste — village by village, with rates assigned and exemptions noted. The survey's results are cut into temple walls, which is why it survives when every later paper record of its kind is gone.
cards.why: The assessment state at full stretch, and the stone copy outlived all the paper ones.
cards.evidence: The Chola survey inscriptions, with their measured extents and soil classes.

cards.what: The lost-wax bronzes reach their peak: Nataraja in the circle of flame, Parvati mid-stride, saints with individuated faces. Each is cast solid for procession — these are gods that travel — and the finest come from a few workshops whose hands scholars can now tell apart.
cards.why: Processional theology in bronze, at a level of casting never surpassed anywhere.
cards.evidence: The dated temple bronzes, their inscriptions of gift, and the workshop attributions.

cards.what: Rajaraja's son takes the machine his father built and points it outward: Sri Lanka held, the Ganges reached, Srivijaya raided, embassies to China. He founds a new capital with a temple to rival his father's and a tank he names the Chola-Ganga.
cards.why: The empire at maximum reach — and every project is also an argument with his father.
cards.evidence: The Tanjore and Gangaikondacholapuram inscriptions, and the Chinese embassy records.

cards.what: Rajendra's armies reach the Ganges, and the campaign's stated trophy is water: pots of it, carried south to fill the new capital's tank. Conquest is performed as pilgrimage, and the tank's name — Chola-Ganga — makes the claim permanent.
cards.why: Sovereignty asserted by hydrology: the sacred river annexed by the jarful.
cards.evidence: The Tiruvalangadu plates and the Gangaikondacholapuram tank inscriptions.

cards.what: Chola missions reach the Song court, are logged by Chinese officials with their gifts and titles, and trade at Quanzhou, where a Tamil merchant community will later build a Shiva temple whose carved stones still exist. State, guild and temple all cross the sea together.
cards.why: The eastern trade at government level, confirmed in the other side's archives.
cards.evidence: The Song dynastic records of Chulian embassies, and the Tamil-inscribed stones at Quanzhou.

cards.what: A Chalukya prince with a Chola mother takes the Chola throne, and two dynasties that fought for a century become one line. The wars over Vengi end in a genealogy rather than a conquest — the mandala resolving itself by marriage.
cards.why: A war ended by inheritance: the succession as diplomatic instrument.
cards.evidence: The Kulottunga inscription series and both dynasties' genealogical claims.

cards.what: The mission logged at the Song court in 1077 is not princes: it is seventy-two merchants, trading sixty thousand strings of cash worth of goods. The state's flag and the guild's capital travel in the same ships, and the Chinese clerks record the arithmetic.
cards.why: Foreign policy conducted by a chamber of commerce, receipted by the other side.
cards.evidence: The Song shi's record of the 1077 Chulian mission and its valuation.

cards.what: A commentary on an old smriti becomes the operating law of most of India: inheritance, partition, the joint family's shares. Seven centuries later the British courts adopt it as the standard, and it governs Hindu property law into the twentieth century.
cards.why: A twelfth-century law commentary still being cited in twentieth-century courtrooms.
cards.evidence: The Mitakshara text and its career in Anglo-Hindu case law.

cards.what: The Lilavati teaches arithmetic through problems addressed to a woman — bees, necklaces, elephants — and the Siddhanta Shiromani works through algebra and astronomy including results at the edge of the calculus. He states plainly that a quantity divided by zero is infinite.
cards.why: The high point of classical Indian mathematics, written to be teachable.
cards.evidence: The texts themselves and their vast commentarial and educational tradition.

cards.what: A cycle of songs on Radha and Krishna — jealousy, separation, reunion — in Sanskrit set to ragas, frankly erotic and read as theology. It enters temple liturgy at Puri, where it is danced nightly, and seeds devotional art from Rajasthan to Assam.
cards.why: The love lyric as scripture, and it has been in continuous performance since.
cards.evidence: The text, the Puri liturgical tradition, and the painting cycles it generated.

cards.what: On star-shaped plans in soft soapstone that hardens with age, the Hoysala workshops carve friezes of unprecedented density — processions of elephants, scrollwork, narrative bands — and the sculptors sign their work. Individual artists' names and titles survive in dozens.
cards.why: Sculpture dense enough to read, by artists who signed it.
cards.evidence: Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura, with their signed sculptures.

cards.what: On a plateau with no perennial river, the Kakatiyas chain thousands of tanks so that one's overflow feeds the next. The inscriptions record who built each and who must maintain it. Most are still in use, which makes this the era's most durable public work.
cards.why: Irrigation as network engineering, and the network is still running.
cards.evidence: The Pakhal, Ramappa and Laknavaram tanks and the maintenance inscriptions.

cards.what: The Kakatiya throne passes to a daughter, who rules as king — the inscriptions use the masculine title — leads armies, and dies, the evidence suggests, on campaign. Marco Polo, passing the coast, reports the kingdom ruled by a queen beloved of her people.
cards.why: A woman ruling as king, in her own inscriptions and a foreign traveller's report.
cards.evidence: The Rudrama inscription series, the Chandupatla memorial inscription, and Polo's account.

cards.what: The line that rebuilt the south, surveyed its land, banked in its temples and shipped embassies to China ends quietly, squeezed between Pandya revival and Hoysala pressure. No sack, no dramatic fall — the inscriptions simply stop accumulating.
cards.why: The focus period closes the way institutions actually end: not with fire, with silence.
cards.evidence: The terminal Chola inscriptions and the Pandya records that succeed them.

cards.what: A temple built as the sun god's chariot: twelve pairs of carved wheels, each a working sundial, seven horses, on a scale so ambitious the main tower eventually fell. What stands is the porch, and it is still one of the largest achievements of Indian building.
cards.why: Architecture as cosmology at maximum scale — and an engineering overreach the ruins admit.
cards.evidence: The Konark complex, its wheel dials, and the construction accounts in the Baya Chakada palm leaves.

cards.what: A mathematician in Kerala derives infinite series for the sine, cosine and arctangent, and with them pi to eleven places — with error terms for truncation. The results reach Europe's textbooks three centuries later under Newton's and Leibniz's names.
cards.why: Core results of the calculus, with proofs, three centuries early, in Malayalam-speaking Kerala.
cards.evidence: The Kerala school texts — Tantrasangraha, Yuktibhasha — crediting Madhava for the series.

cards.what: The Ahom state keeps chronicles as an administrative duty: officials write the buranjis, in Ahom and then Assamese, recording campaigns, embassies, prices and floods, continuously for six centuries. No other Indian polity institutionalised its own history-keeping this way.
cards.why: History as a department of government, kept up for six hundred years.
cards.evidence: The surviving buranji corpus and its use in reconstructing the Ahom state.

cards.what: A revenue clerk's son from the Punjab emerges from an experience at the river saying there is no Hindu and no Musalman, and spends decades travelling and teaching: one God, honest work, shared food, and the uselessness of ritual without conduct. Communities form around the hymns.
cards.why: A tradition founded on the refusal of the era's central boundary.
cards.evidence: The janamsakhi accounts, and Nanak's own compositions preserved in the Adi Granth.

cards.what: Babur brings matchlocks and field guns behind a barricade of chained carts, with cavalry wheeling from the flanks. The Lodi army, many times larger, breaks against it in a morning. The military economics of the subcontinent change in one battle.
cards.why: Gunpowder decides an Indian field battle for the first time, and every state must now afford it.
cards.evidence: The Baburnama's own tactical account, and the battle's aftermath in the Delhi succession.
cards.becomes: The Mughal empire — and a two-century arms race in cannon, matchlocks and the revenue systems to pay for them.

cards.what: The Deccan sultanates combine, the imperial army loses in a day, and the city — one of the largest in the world — is abandoned and stripped over months. The site never recovers; the dynasty retreats south and dwindles. Travellers a generation later describe streets of ruins.
cards.why: The fall of the last great southern empire, fast enough that its capital simply stops.
cards.evidence: Ferishta and the Portuguese accounts, and the destruction layer across the excavated city.
cards.becomes: The Deccan sultanates inherit the plateau; the Nayakas inherit the south and run Vijayanagara's administration under their own names for two more centuries.

cards.what: The emperor builds a house for religious argument and staffs it ecumenically: ulema, Jesuits from Goa, Jains, Zoroastrians, and eventually the emperor's own syncretic conclusions. The Jesuits' letters home record their frustration at being heard politely and not converted.
cards.why: A state running comparative religion as court procedure.
cards.evidence: The Akbarnama and Badauni's hostile account, and the Jesuit mission correspondence.

cards.what: Akbar's revenue system measures the land, averages ten years of prices and yields, and fixes cash rates per crop per district. The Ain publishes the schedules. It is the most sophisticated fiscal machine of its century anywhere, and the Company later builds directly on its records.
cards.why: The empire's real constitution is its revenue table.
cards.evidence: The Ain-i-Akbari's dastur schedules and the surviving Mughal revenue documents.

cards.what: Potosi's silver crosses the world and much of it ends in India, paid for cloth, pepper and indigo, because India sells more than it buys and takes the difference in metal. The Mughal mints turn the inflow into rupees; European writers complain for two centuries about the drain eastward.
cards.why: Before the Drain ran out of India, one ran into it, and it was global silver.
cards.evidence: Mughal mint-output series, and the European trade companies' bullion-export records and complaints.

cards.what: The Mughal empire, at its height, invades Assam repeatedly for seventy years, and loses — to river warfare, monsoon logistics, and a state that can mobilise labour without cash through the paik system. The buranjis record every campaign; so, more briefly, do the Mughal chroniclers.
cards.why: The empire that took everything else could not take the Brahmaputra valley.
cards.evidence: The buranji and Mughal accounts of the campaigns, agreeing on outcomes if not on emphasis.

cards.what: At the river narrows below Guwahati, the Ahom commander — ill, and having executed his own uncle for slackness on the earthworks — forces a naval battle in the channel where Mughal numbers cannot deploy, and breaks the fleet. The frontier settles at the Manas for good.
cards.why: The battle that fixed the empire's eastern limit, won on water by a dying man.
cards.evidence: The buranji accounts and the Mughal record of the retreat.

cards.what: The emperor moves south in 1681 and never returns: a generation of sieges against Maratha forts, each taken and retaken, while the jagir system buckles under the cost and officers wait years for assignments. He dies in camp, the treasury drained, the enemy intact.
cards.why: The campaign that won every siege and lost the empire.
cards.evidence: The Mughal court chronicles and campaign correspondence, and the fiscal collapse documented in the assignment records.

cards.what: Portugal cannot conquer the Indian Ocean's trade, so it licenses it: sail with a purchased pass, calling at Portuguese forts, or be lawful prize. The system is enforced by a handful of ships against a vast commerce, and it works because artillery at sea has no local answer.
cards.why: The ocean acquires a toll gate, and free navigation ends for three centuries.
cards.evidence: The Portuguese pass registers and prize records, and Indian and Ottoman correspondence protesting the system.

cards.what: The Nawab of Awadh, the Mughal emperor and the deposed Nawab of Bengal combine against the Company and lose in an afternoon at Buxar. The treaty that follows gives the Company the diwani — the revenue of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa — with the emperor's own seal on the grant.
cards.why: Plassey was a conspiracy; Buxar was a verdict. After it the Company is a power, not a firm.
cards.evidence: The battle and the Treaty of Allahabad of 1765, with the diwani grant.
cards.becomes: Revenue collection by a joint-stock company, the drain of bullion reversed, and the fiscal base for every later conquest.

cards.what: William Jones, a judge in Calcutta, founds a society for Asian studies and announces that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin are sprung from a common source. Comparative philology begins; so does the systematic European engagement with Indian texts — editing, translating, and appropriating.
cards.why: The discovery that Europe and India share a language family, made in a Calcutta courtroom's spare time.
cards.evidence: Jones's third anniversary discourse of 1786, and the Asiatick Researches series.

cards.what: Type is cut for Bengali, Devanagari, Tamil and the rest, and presses at Serampore and Calcutta begin producing grammars, scriptures and newspapers. The cost of a copy falls to almost nothing. For the corpus, this is the event after which loss becomes reversible.
cards.why: The knowledge economy's endgame: from here, a text printed is a text that cannot easily die.
cards.evidence: The Serampore Mission Press records, Panchanan Karmakar's typefaces, and the vernacular press explosion that followed.

cards.what: Every ten years the state counts everyone, and sorts them: by religion, by caste, by occupation, by language. Categories that were fluid, local and negotiable become printed, ranked and permanent. Petitions immediately begin arriving asking to be reclassified upward.
cards.why: The count creates what it claims to describe: enumeration hardens identity.
cards.evidence: The census reports from 1871 onward, and the caste-ranking petitions in their appendices.

cards.what: The famines of 1876-78 and the 1890s kill on a scale the export tables make unbearable to read — grain leaves famine districts by rail throughout. Commissions follow, and produce the Famine Codes: trigger criteria, relief works, wage scales. The codes save lives later; the tables remain.
cards.why: The state learns to manage famine after declining to prevent it, and both facts are in its own records.
cards.evidence: The Famine Commission reports, the provincial codes, and the grain export statistics for the famine years.

cards.what: Sepoy regiments rise at Meerut, take Delhi, and proclaim the old emperor; a year of war follows, atrocious on both sides. When it ends, the Company is abolished, the Crown assumes India directly, annexation-by-lapse stops, and the army is permanently restructured.
cards.why: The end of company rule, and the beginning of the state the freedom movement would face.
cards.evidence: The military and civil records of 1857-58, the trial of Bahadur Shah Zafar, and the Government of India Act 1858.

cards.match: Bengal is partitioned, and the swadeshi
cards.what: The province is split, officially for administrative convenience, transparently along religious lines. The response invents the movement toolkit: boycott of British goods, swadeshi manufacture, national schools, songs. The partition is annulled in 1911; the toolkit is permanent.
cards.why: The techniques of the next forty years of nationalism are invented in this one campaign.
cards.evidence: The partition and annulment orders, the boycott statistics, and the swadeshi movement's own literature.

cards.what: Gandhi walks two hundred and forty miles to the sea with seventy-eight companions and picks up untaxed salt. The act is trivial, universal and photogenic: everyone uses salt, anyone can break this law, and the state must either ignore defiance or arrest tens of thousands. It arrests tens of thousands.
cards.why: Civil disobedience engineered as spectacle, with the law chosen precisely for its absurdity.
cards.evidence: The march's daily record, the mass arrests and the Gandhi-Irwin pact that followed.

cards.what: Rice prices spiral in a war economy — denial policies, lost Burmese imports, hoarding, and a government that prioritises Calcutta's war industries. There is no overall shortage of food in India that year. Around three million die. The Famine Inquiry's own report concedes the failure was administrative.
cards.why: The century's worst Indian famine happened amid sufficient food. The mechanism was priority, not weather.
cards.evidence: The Famine Inquiry Commission report, the price and procurement series, and the shipping records.
cards.dispute: Responsibility remains fiercely argued — between wartime cabinet decisions, provincial government failure and market dynamics. The records support a heavier and a lighter reading of London's role, and both are published.

cards.what: Three years of drafting and debate, recorded verbatim across twelve volumes: federalism, language, minorities, untouchability, all argued in the open by members including fourteen women. The result adopts universal adult franchise at a stroke, for the largest electorate ever created.
cards.why: The campaign's last artefact: the argument itself, published, and the reader lives inside its outcome.
cards.evidence: The Constituent Assembly Debates and the calligraphed and illustrated original document.
